Kid Chocolate, The Cuban bon
bon and former teatherweight
champion of the world, took
another step toward a shot at the
worlds lightweight crown, when he
knocked out Andre Sarilla, Pan
anna gamecock, in the seventh of
a scheduled ten-round bout at
Griffith Stadium last night, be-
fore 1000 satisfied customers.


Chocolates greatest skill and
speed wore Sarilla down and
softened him for the knockout.
Throughout the seven rounds the
"Keed" danced around Sarilla
shooting terrific swings and upper
cuts.


To open the first round Choco-
late let loose a series of right and
left uppercuts that led the spec
tators to believe that he was 60
ing to make short work of Sarilla.
But the Panamanian was tough.
In the second stanZa Chocolate
was less impressive and Sarilla
more aggressive.


Third Round Even


The third round was about even
but from this point on Chocolate
began to wear the Panama boy
down. In the fifth round Sarilla
was a bloody sight. In the sixth
round he was groggy and his right
eye almost closed. The "Keed"
Embossed a series of swift right
and left punches to start the
seventh round and Sarilla toppled
to the floor, kayoed.


Several Cuban and Panamanlan
embassies officials saw the scrap.
Chocolate weighed in at 132
pounds and Sarilla 1870.


The semifinal bout between
Bobby Perry, of Atlantic City, and
Canada Lee, of New York, Choco-
late's stable mate, went eight
rounds as scheduled, with Lee get
ting the decision. Both were
featherweights, and the boy from
the seashore put up game fight
but lacked the punch to win. Lee
floored the Atlantic City opponent
in the fourth round.

shipping two big automobiles from the
royal garage to King Prajadhipok in
London, it was revealed yesterday.

cate the monarch proposes to prolong
his stay abroad, with the probability
of abandoning his decision to abdicate
becoming more remote than ever.

calmly awaiting a government an

government on its part was providing
the masses with plentiful entertain
ment. Public lotteries and other diver
sions were announced

abdicate unless the government re-
tracted its action abolishing the royal
sanction for death penalties.

services, such as housing, health pro-
motion and general welfare activities

taxes and demanded reductions.

Senate and House confereeS last
night agreed on the administration
requested Indian policy bill, virtually
assuring enactment.

version was adopted in the main.

troverted item in the much modified
bill-that providing State laws shall
govern inheritance of Indian lands.

contended was tantamount to deny
ing the Indian inheritance privileges

Indians

was the House provision requiring
the Secretary of the Interior to call
elections on the different reservations

dians to decide by a majority vote

new law.

the eastern coast Of England. where
cliffs are slowly crumbling into the un-
resting surf and carrying with them
buildings that were once standing far
from any imagined danger, says the
Boston Transcript.


However, in England q compensating
process Is going on, for the western shore
Of the island Is gaining on the sea and
In some places fshermen's cottages that
used to be just few steps above high
tide are now so far from the waters
edge that the fishermen grumble. They
are not walking tribe and like to live
where they can have their kedge-anchor
hooked round a leg Of the breakfast
table.


Now, there is a tradition along the
British Channel that long before Caesar
invaded Britain people could pass from
that island into France dry-Shod. The
same process of erosion that Is year by
year eating into the chalk cliffs facing
the North Sea, gradually grooved a
strait from the North Sea to the Allan
tic ocean, and the present English
Channel covers the footpaths that once
criss-crossed the low plain between Kent
and Picardy.


The theory has been advanced that
the British Isles are being cut of more
and more from the European continent
by the sea, and being built up to the
westward, and that eventually they will
cross the Atlantic and turn up at our
very doors-unless, indeed. our own
eastern coast should by that time have
sunk out Of sight beneath the waves
while our dominions along the Pacific
have built up a new littoral, leaving
Hollywood and Malibu Beach about

Commodity prices during the past

Only 4 out Of IA groups registered

distribution has steadily advanced

peak for this year was reached in the
third week of March and since that
time the weekly index has registered
six consecutive declines.


Industrial prices declined, following
a high for the year a week ago. The
underlying trend, however. has moved
upward with little interruption since
February year ago.


Farm Prices Down.


Agricultural prices lost more ground
than any other group. Cotton, in
particular, was weak, breaking under
the 11-cent level. Wheat, barley and
eggs also averaged lower, which more
than counteracted the moderate
strength noted in corn, oats, rye, flax
seed and butter.


Live stock prices moved upward
slightly, rejecting some gain in the
price average of hogs and lambs. Cat
tie prices failed to register strength
during the week.


Building materials climbed to a
new high, due to the price mark-up
In nails.


Non-ferrous metals failed to gain,
the index averaging lower than a
week ago. Copper and lead held the
gains recorded earlier in the month

declined sharply, carrying the price
average down.

ward following the unusually broad

BALTIMORE, June 16-Four new

trial Bureau of the Baltimore Asso-

Two are clothing concerns one will
engage in the refining Of fish OIL
while the fourth will engage in COM
mercial printing The expansions are
also varied, being made by concerns
engaged in milk pasteurization, meat
packing, clothing and tin containers


Business indiceS in this report
show substantial increases over similar
periods OF last year. with the excep-
ton of building contracts" H. Findlay
French, director of the bureau. said.
"The building permits for May were
stimulated by major municipal
project, but the fact that only 80
houses were permitted uululg UIlt lllSl

report, the Industrial Bureau COM
pletes the fifteenth year of its activi-

The years since 1919 include two

preston, but at all times it has been

TOR about six months Mr. Bulwinkle had
gone without lunches, hoping that he could
put aside enough of the lunch money and what
he, with a clear conscience, might hold back
from commissions in order to open little real
estate office of his own. But that dream, while
never completely fading from his memory, had
finally fed from his hopes.


Once, long ago when Mary was only chick.
he had told her of his dream. 1t was like tell
ing almost no one at all to tell little Mary and
yet it had helped when her thin little arms
had been flung around his neck and in
ecstasy of glee she had squealed: "Oh, Pop!
Cee Pop"


And now that this should happen when real
estate had just taken turn for the better and
the children were not even on their own feetl
Mr.. Bulwinkle, sitting there crotchety and dis
tracted, ground toe into the pebble walk and
felt the fine stones cut through the cardboard
hole-covering of his shoe and into his foot. He
and Mary together had discovered the art of
covering shoe holes with paper.


Mary had said, Gee, Pop you just couldn't
walk in shoes you didn't pay for, could you?
I mean. that's why you don't buy yourself
things. isn't it? I mean, you'd be afraid you'd
fall down and break your neck something,
wouldn't you?" And after that Mary had
taken care of the neighbors' babies and had
solicited magazine subscriptions and with the
money she had made she had bought him a
pair of shoes. She had written on the card,
On account of its almost Winter Pop, and
you'd never get them yourself. Lovingly, your
daughter, Mary"


Mamma had gone into tantrums of humiliation
when she had found out about the neighbors'
babies and the magazines. She had ratified
off in her thin furious voice just what she
thought of such carrying on, and to further i'm
press 1t on the culprit, she had slapped Marys
round little cheeks. Mary had taken 1t all
silently, respectfully. standing very straight.
But she hadn't been so calm inside for she
had locked herself in her room afterward and
hadn't ventured out in two days. Mr. Bull
winkle had worn little path up and down
outside of her door, aching to 60 in and take
the sobbing little thing in his arms but always
there was the thought Of Mamma and the tan
trum Mamma could go into If Mamma was
crossed.


At O'Clock that evening the Bulwinkle
family was gathered around the dinner table
and Josie, girl who had been with the Bull
wrinkles only two weeks, serving the table.
Josie was in none too affable mood She had
Just heard that the Bulwinkles kept maid
week or two and then discharged her, without
pay for impudence, inadequate service, accused
theft, something.


Mrs Bulwinkle had learned at a book review
tea that afternoon that the firm Of Theoter &
Caulk was definitely washed up. When Mamma
lifted quizzical. neatly plucked eyebrow and
asked Mr.. Bulwinkle about it, all the childrens
papa's face. Mr.. Bulwinkle only swallowed
very Deep and said: "Rumors, my dear. Pure
rumors. The Office will reopen in few days"
Only Mary noticed how the soup spoon trem-
bled in the prominently veined hands.

The present lawsuit over these rail-

gress' power to take such action.


The Federal Court of st. Louis has

old gold clauses are uncomfortable.

The upward surge of activity in
the steel industry has gathered
added momentum, the weekly Iron
Age Review says today, with ingot
production placed at Al per cent
of capacity, a gain of 212 points
from week ago, and the highest
operating rate since last August.


Some Reactionary Influences


Reactionary influences are Sc
we're weather conditions which
have held back building opera
tions, and sporadic labor difficult
ties, especially among automotlVe
plants in the Chicago district.


Scrap prices are stronger IN
virtually all centers, and ad-
vances in heavy melting steel at
chicago and Pittsburgh have
raised the Iron Age scrap COM
posite from $12.25 to $12.75 a
gross ton, it's highest level since
october, 1880. At Chicago, local
scarcity of heavy melting grade
is forcing the trade to draw upon
the St. Louis district for supplies.


Demand from the motor car
industry shows no abatement and
is reflected in the heavy book
ings of sheet and strip producers.

down orders for cold-finished
sheets and enameling stock, as
their capacities for these grades
are fully taken up for March.

Retail orders for automobiles
now exceed so days capacity pro
duction and are in the largest
volume since 1929.


Steel bookings from the auto
mobile sector are being supple
mented by broadening demands
from other sources. Mills are
commencing to get releases from
the Pennsylvania railroad against
the purchase of $4,000 tons for
car construction. as well as its
orders for electrification work.


Specifications for the $4,000

ingen cars are being prepared

this week or early next week.

THOSE who labeled the recent


embargo on arms exports to


Cuba "a, new expression of
Il the good-neighbor policy"


showed little acquaintance
with conditions in the island republic
and even less knowledge of Latin
American politics and psychology.


Official spokesmen and editorial
writer's who have praised the presi-
Dental embargo-which allows only
the Cuban government to buy arms
in the United States-have given
two reason for it: First, that it is
going to bring about internal peace
in Cuba and end several months Of
constant political unrest, and, second,
that, because of that, it will enhance
the prestige of the "good-neighbor'
policy and increase Cuban and Latin
American good will toward the United
States.


When Grau San Martin was forced
out a few months ago and Col.
Mendieta installed in Office, with OBJ
vious Washington support. the claim
was also made that Mendieta's hasty
recognition, despite its evident par
tiality, was to result in the conSolida-
tion of domestic peace in Cuba. 1t
did not, of course, and neither will
the embargo.


Cubans Not Satisfied.


What Washington observers over
looked then, and what they seem to
;e hn Cr1honc
themselves are not satisfied with the
conservative Mendieta regime. The
Cuban masses not only dislike the
Mendieta government for its reac-
tionary character and its inability to
bring immediate economic relief, but
they are particularly bitter against
it because they realize that it stands
in the way of the completion of their
revolution, the revolution they
started last year by overthrowing
Distator- President Machado.


In the eyes Of the Cuban masses,
Col Mendieta, like Senor de Cespedes
before him, is stealing their revolu-
ton. Both are trusted, honest men,
but they are of the old guard, who
have never sympathized with the new
aspirations and the new trends OF
the younger Cuba.


The Cespedes regime, which fol-
lowed Machado's fall, was the usual
stopgap liberal coalition and it was
born with the original sin of almost
undisclosed Washington Endorsement.
1t could not have lasted long. And
it did not. The situation soon proved
too big for it, and a coup of young
intellectuals and non-commissioned
officers. in the army which surprised
every one abroad, and Washington
more than any one, but which could
not have surprised the Cuban people,
gave new hope to the masses.


Fear that the new government
might go to far to the left and
create international complications,
the pressure of American business in
terests in the island and certain per-
sonal influences, however, kept the
Washington administration from rec
ognizing the Grau San Martin
regime. The fact that it maintained
internal order for four months and
kept all its foreign obligations was
not sufficient to convince skeptical
and interested foreign observers.


Quick Recognition.


Yet when Col. Mendieta succeeded
Grau San Martin, few hours was
all the State Department needed to
find out that the Mendieta govern
ment had popular support and could
preserve domestic peace. Col. Men
dieta was Immediately recognized,
but only to confront, of course, con-
tinued unrest and increasing violence.

GARY, Ind, April IA Pl.-Joe
Ferrara, known as Gary's perpetual
candidate, today got court order to
remove his name from the ballot for
the May 8 election.


Ferrara, although never successful,
has frequently run for mayor and
other Offices during the last 10 years.
He was highly indignant today, how
ever, when he discovered his name
had been filed as a candidate for
trustee of Calumet Township on the
Democratic ticket.


The difficulty was that Ferrara's
daughter, Mary, also was candidate
for the Office. On his plea that the
petition filed for him contained a
forged signature, the court ordered
his name off the ballot.

SALT LAKE CITY, Utah, January
13.-More than 1000 adults, men and
women. are improving their time
through free training afforded them by
the G. w. A. This State always has
been noted for its educational facilities.
Last Fall, however, about $50 teachers,
well qualified and willing to work, found
themselves without pupils to teach.
Curtailment had not been drastic, but
some had been necessary. Now, more
than half of those teachers who were
without jobs are employed. They are
helping those who didn't have a
chance or who did not take advantage
of that chance when it was available.
At any rate. these grown-up school boys
and girls seem to appreciate the op-
portunity offered them now.


Subjects taught offer wide range.
The following are included: Art, book

matics, economics, English, foreigners

TIVOLI, N. Y, October 29.-Her
New York tour interrupted by death,
Mrs. Franklin D. Roosevelt remained
in this little Hudson Valley town for
the funeral today of Valentine Hall,
81, her uncle and one-time tennis star.


It was Valentine Hall who taught
her to ride and play tennis when
Eleanor Roosevelt, 10 years old and
orphaned, came to stay with her
grandmother, Mrs. Valentine Hall. Her
uncle was 20 then.


Death came to the uncle late Friday
night, about the time Mrs. Roosevelt
finished her upstate campaign tour
for Mrs. Caroline O'Day, Democratic
candidate for Congress-at-large, at
Albany. The Presidents wife learned
of it when she stopped at the hand
some family home overlooking the
Hudson Saturday morning.


She had come to visit her uncle on
her way to her own home, Hyde Park,
20 miles farther south, but she re-
manned to help arrange for his funeral
instead.

NEW YORK. August 4.--With some
of the leading rail shares back around
their lowest prices recorded this year,
traders who follow chart theories were
inclined to desert the bull side of
stocks today to wait for a test Of the
late July low points. Rails have
shown little rallying power the last
week and have acted as q drag on
the general list.


However, the contraction OF trad
ing on the decline yesterday and the
scattered nature of liquidation at the
week end reassured analysts who as
sumed the market had plumbed its
midsummer depths on the sharp
break Of July 26.


Reports that rate experts studying
plans for petition for higher freight
rates were considering restricting the
increase to heavy classifications, such
as coal, to dissipate pessimism over
the railroads plight. A coal rate
boost, for instance, would not aid
Western carriers much. They are
faced with loss of freight as result
Of crop failures and drought damage.
On the contrary, it would help some
of the carriers that least need it, such
as the Norfolk & Western and the
Chesapeake & Ohio.


Worked out on a seasonally ad-
justed basis, the railroad car loadings
index for the week ended July 28 was
at the lowest point touched this year,
having sagged slowly in recent
months. Thus not much hope was
held out that July railroad earnings
statements would make a better show
ing than the June statements, the
source of much of the bearishness
surrounding railroad shares lately.


Railroads last month curtailed
maintenance work in an effort to off,
set higher costs. but 1t was considered
doubtful that they could do much in
that direction. Summary of the June
earnings statements published recent
ly indicates that whereas gross reve-
nue. for the month increased less than
2 per cent compared with the same
month last year. operating expenses
were more than 10 per cent higher
and cut down net operating income
substantially.

BY FLORENCE LA GANKE.


A GROUP Of college girls who knew


Peters sister well and belonged to
the same sorority were having the best
time at a party given by Dorothy, an
other sorority sister.


The girls had been invited to play
bridge. They came, eager to see each
other again and to hear all the latest
Summer gossip. Then they had to dis
cuss the coming year at college and
compare notes on courses they would
and would not take. Grace. who had
finished college last June, said she en-
We'd the girls another year back at the
dear old school, but some way she did
not seem to be as downhearted as she

During the evening and before the
refreshments were served messenger
boy brought o sheaf of kilograms.

self.


1t was not until later that the group
remembered that Grace made no offer
to read hers aloud, but waited until
all the others had been opened.

Pepys." The girls caught on at once
for they knew what an inveterate old

new ring?" and the secret was out.

ment to a well-known bachelor who

home on the beach front.

NANTES, France, October 26.-A
definite break with Premier CASTOR
Doumergue's truce government drew
one step nearer yesterday as the
powerful Radical Socialist party's
Committee on Constitutional Revision
voted to reject the premier's demand
for changes to deprive the Senate
of power to dissolve the Chamber.

accepts most of the premier's plan, but
refuses its main point, was presented
to the Congress. Vote will be taken
tomorrow or Sunday.

stitutional provision center around his
proposal that the premier or the
President, or both, be given authority
to dissolve the Chamber and call for
election. the Radical Socialists re-
fusal to support him might mean the
wreck of his government.


Edouard Herriot and five other
Radical Socialists are, members of
Doumergue's cabinet and their resig-
nations almost certainly would force
the government out.

While naval ceremony and fam
fare over the Presidents departure
aboard the Houston last evening were
cut to minimum. small pleasure
craft in Chesapeake Bay gave him
a royal send-off, accompanied by their
sirens, horns and whistles, with anna
teur shippers maneuvering their boats
as close to the big cruiser and the
two deStroyers as their knowledge
and their sometimes splitting motors
permitted.


AS early as S pm. two hours and
a half before the President left the
dock at the Naval Academy. pleasure
craft we're gathering around the
Houston. which lay at anchor about
seven miles out from Annapolis in the
bay. Most of them spent the time
circling the cruiser. and sailor sta
toned at the flag aft on the Houston
had a busy afternoon acknowledging
their salutes. An excursion steamer,
Baltimore bound, passed within few
yards of the big ship and the excur-
sionists, who packed her decks, ex-
changed noisy greetings with the gobs.


Early Preparations.


Preparations to receive the Presi-
dent aboard the Houston began hours
before the President reached Annapo-
lis. Sailors on the cruiser formed at
their stations and were inspected by
their officers, then stood at ease. A
subchaSer put out from Annapolis with
movie men aboard and new activity
began aboard the Houston. AS the
subchaSer came alongside, signals were
exchanged and the crew of the Hous-
ton manned the rail while the sub
chaser circled the ship several times,
movie cameras grinding away.


The flotilla of small boatS-ranging
from large pleasure yachts to couple
of row boats with outboard motors and
containing a pretty fair representa-
ton of the craft of Chesapeake Bay
moved in closer to the cruiser while
the ceremony for the movies was in
progress. Then, when the subchaser
moved off. a long wait of an hour
and a half began. The Houston's
crew remained lined up at the rails,
and the officers stood at the starboard
Underwriting.


The ships band undertook a con-
cert. The small boats shippers Shut
off their throbbing motors and after
each tune the spectators applauded.
Finally the band got tired and quit.
The sun set over Annapolis. sharply
bringing the Naval Academy dome.
the church steeples and the State
House into dark silhouette against a
patch of crimson sky.


The Houston pulled down her flag.
while the sailors stood at salute. All
the small craft pulled down their
flags. The cruisers riding lights
went on-and all the small craft
turned theirs on.


Steams Into Position.


The destroyer Williamson, anchored
some distance from the Houston,
pulled up her hook and steamed
slowly into position nearer the cruiser.
Far of toward Annapolis the running
lights of the Gilmer, which had re-
ceived the President aboard at the
Academy dock, could be seen moving
against the darker background of the
city's skyline.


The Gilmer steamed slowly seaward
in the narrow Annapolis harbor chan
nel then turned and made large
circle which brought her into posi-
ton to come up alongside the Hous-
ton. She steamed very slowly. the
small boats making room, and tied
up. Small boats maneuvered fran
tically to get into position to see the
President-and failed, so close were
the two ships together. The Presi-
dent stepped from the destroyer's
deck to the cruiser while boatswain
piped and the sailors stood stifdy at
attention. Some skipper blasted a
greeting with his siren, and the small
boats took it up. Then the Gilmer
backed slowly away, after warning
toot from her whistle A few minutes
later the Houston's anchor was pulled
up, her running lights showed and
she steamed slowly south, followed
by her conveying destroyers. The
f1otilla of small boats disbanded, some
heading up the Bay for Baltimore,
others heading South toward Thomas
Light and the Bay resorts, others
returning to Annapolis.

CHICAGO. August 25.-Those dar-
ing young gals in their flying machine
took their Saturday night sponge"
as they swung along with the breeze
over Curtiss- Reynolds Airport tonight,
hunting q new endurance flight record
at the end of endless circles.


The Lone Star, Jean La Rene
and Mary Elizabeth Owens Of Texas,
taking turns at the stick and the air
mattress, was two days out Of port at
8:13 o'clock tonight and churning the
same air channel merrily, eight days
to go for a new women's record.


Minor mishaps have dented but
not daunted the girls.


Slashing away at q rope that
dangled their basket of food from
the "mothering" plane above, Mary
sliced her finger with the knife. but
she didn't stop at drug store.


Again the refueling plane SKINNED

parachute whose ripcord Jean had in
advertently pulled as she answered
the bugle this morning. Mary stuck
her head through the roof and put
herself in receptive mood and stance
to pick the heavy bag Of silk out Of
the air.


Suddenly cross-current swung the
chute around and 1t struck the girl
on the head, knocking her goggles and
helmet of. She was bit dazed but
not damaged.


Miss Phoebe Stein of Oak Park is
their dietician.


Irish Stew and fried chicken" is
what they like, she said, though since
they don't get much exercise I send
up less meat and more vegetables" !"
Aspirin and smelling salts are also on
the bill of fare, but they haven't
proved necessary yet.


Kenneth Hanter, who set the mems
record in 1890 at 554 hours and As
minutes, pilots the refueling ship and
superintended the tuning of the Lone
Star before she started Willing the
hours away over Curtiss Field. He
radiated confidence tonight that the
girls would even pass his own mark.

BY the Associated Press.


NEW YORK. September 2s.-The
Empire States party lines were drawn
strictly over the issue Of the New
Deal" as Democrats and Republicans
launched tonight their crucial Fall
campaigns in President Roosevelt's
home commonwealth.


Delegates to the parties State con-
ventions returned to their home dis
tricts with the coming fight sharply
defined by Numerically opposed plat
forms.


The State Democracy plunged into
the campaign with ringing indorse-
ment of President Roosevelt's policies
and the party's high leaders instruct
ing their lieutenants to battle for
votes on the national administration
record.


G. o. p. Condemns Doctrines.


The Republicans. under control Of
"Old Guard" factions, joined the is
sues firmly by condemntng the basic
doctrines of the Democratic high
command and putting forth proposals,
many of which were in direct conflict
with the ruling party's policies.


State issues were given only sec
ondary attention, but the Democrats
served notice they would make capi-
tai out of charges by the deposed Re
publican chairman, w. Kingsland
Macy, that his own party was dom
mated" by public utility interests.


In contrast with the stormy fac
tional strife in their opponents ranks,
the Democrats were in almost COM
plete accord, renominating their en-
tire ticket, headed by Senator Royal
S. Copeland and Gov. Herber5 H.
Lehman.


Macy Voted Out.


Anti-Macy forces-the Old Guard
went into the Republican convention
with the same dominant strength
shown earlier in meetings of the State
Committee. Headed by F. Trubee Da-
vison, former Assistant Secretary of
War, they ruled the convention and
afterward voted Macy out Of the
Craftsmanship, as had been antici-
pated.


They nominated for Governor the
commissioner of New York City
parks, Robert Moses, who served as
Secretary of State under former Gov
ernor Alfred E. Smith, and has been
one of the Happy Warriors" conf
dants and advisers. The senatorial
nomination went to E. Harold Cluett,
Rensselaer, manufacturer, after at
least two others had declined the des-
ignation.


The Democrats entered the cam
paign, with Postmaster General James
A. Farley again heading the State
Committee.


Democrats Blame Hoover.


The Democratic platform laid o.
the administration of Herbert Hoove-
the entire blame for conditions ex
isting when President Roosevelt took
Office. It declared uncompromisingly
for the continuation of New Deal
policies and accepted without reserva-
ton the Roosevelt leadership as the
prevailing issue before the voters.


The Republican Resolutions Com
mittee specifically credited the Roose-
velt administration for some "help-
full and constructive" measures but
differed vigorously on most Of its basic
policies.

MEMPHIS, Tenn, August 81
People are beginning to shake their
heads and say Alma Higginbotham
has death jinxed.


Alma, aged 10, was burning paper
in the back yard of her home We'd
nesday when there was loud pop.
She thought it was a light bulb.
There was another pop, possibly a
bang, and she clutched at her throat.


A shell struck her on the windpipe.
Physicians say If the .38-caliber bullet
had been pointed in her direction, 1t
would have gone through the wind
pipe and crashed into the spine.


Things happen like that in Alma's
life. Five years ago she hurried from
the attic of her home for dinner, trip
ped and dived through glass door.
She got of with minor cuts.


When she was years old a neigh
Dor boy struck her with a sharp rock.
The point bored into her skull, stop
ping a fraction of an inch from the
brain. She was soon at play again.


She was still in the toddling stage
when she was swinging high on a
grapevine. The grapevine broke,
hurtling her 80 feet. A little atten-
ton and she was ready for new ad-
ventures.

DETROIT, Sept. % G.N.SO.
The white-robed priests Of st.
Dominic chanted a solemn requiem
mass over the body of 11-year-old
Lillian Gallaher today, while the
nationwide manhunt for her mad
slayer went on without success.


Merton Word Goodrich, thin.
faced Ohio maniac, in whose apart
ment the girls mutilated body
was found stuffed in a trunk, was
reported seen at a dozen widely
separated points. But, as each
clue was run down and found to
be false, the fugitive and his Grip
pied wife, Margaret, remained at
liberty.


Classmates Sob


Iillian's classmates Of st. Doml-
MICS School attended her funeral
mass, and during the intervals
of silence between the solemn
Latin hymns Of the Catholic
funeral ritual, childish SobS were
plainly audible throughout the
crowded church. The child's body
was in q white casket, sealed at the
county morgue. Only Lillian'S
older brother, who identified her,
and the officials Of the morgue,
were permitted to see her body.


It was while selling 10-cent
chances" on a punchboard for
the benefit Of the school that
Lillian apparently was enticed
into Goodrich's apartment only
a few steps from busy Wood
ward Avenue, and there assaulted
and slain.


The punch board, with its
legend. "For a good cause!" was
found, twisted and broken, near
her body. She had sold one
chance"


Believed in Ohio


The impression prevailed among
Detroit police officials that Good
rich and his wife are somewhere
in Ohio. Goodrich has friends
in several Ohio cities including
Elyria, Youngstown and Cleve.
land. Mrs. Goodrich attended
school in Lorain.


Police favored the theory that
the two either drove to Ohio
after the Staying or crossed Lake
Erie on a Cleveland steamer.
They have been reported seen
both on . Cleveland-bound ship
and in an automobile on the Ohio
highway.

text:
North Atlantic winter
weather is a wicked enemy of
sea-faring men. It's most savage
fury is vented on the service,
which long ago earned the right
to be called "The Good Sa-
maritan Of the Sea-" the United
States Coast Guard. When Bit
ter gales come whistling down
from the north, lashing the
ocean to 4O-foot waves; when
snow and sleet flies, and ice
chokes dangerous channels;
when few vessels move except
the great liners, then comes
the time of the Coast Guards
greatest activity.


Straight out into the snaps
ping jaws of the blizzard move
the stout little vessels, bound
on their errands of mercy, to
rescue lives in desperate peril.


Call of Distress


All up and down the Atlantic
coast, from Baltimore to Maine,
Coast Guard cutters have been
keeping the channels open in
every important harbor. And
almost every day one or more
of the ice-breakerS is suddenly
summoned to the rescue Of a
ship in distress. Such was the
call that came to the Coast
Guard Cutter Mendoza, just a
few days ago.


The steamship Maiden Cross
was snoring northWard through
a gale, when she sighted the
windjammer Purneu T. White, a
big lumber schooner from down
East. Terrifically hammered by
the storm, the schooner had
gone on her beam ends, snapped
off her masts like matches, and
lost her sails. She was in a bad
way. All this was radioed by
the Maiden Cross to the cutter
Mendoza, and when he got the
tale the Mendota's skipper,
Comdr. William Keester, stood
out through the lashing gale for
the Chesapeake Lightship.


From the northwest the wind
came with a battering drive.
dropping the temperature to
under zero, sheathing the Men
dota with ice. But, even so, she
found the derelict windjammer,
helpless and waterlogged, got a
line aboard her, and took her in
tow. Then through the wicked
night came a crimson flash from
the schooner's deck, and that
meant just one thing, the
schooner was sinking and there
was no time to lose. Yet, no
boat could possibly live in those
great, gray-green Swells.


Yet, something had to be
done, and through the bowling
of the storm came the shrilling
of the boSun's whistle, calling
all hands to quarters. Coast
GuardSmen thronged the fore
castle, ready for action with
heaving lines. life lines, life
buoys, life RATS, and a gun for
firing life lines. To within 80
feet of the slowly rolling
schooner, the Mendoza worked
through the storm and seas.
Over the schooner she shot
life line, followed by a three
inch hawser and a life raft.


A seaman from the schooner
slid down the hawser to the
raft and was hauled safely
aboard the cutter. Two more

MOUNT AIRY, Md, March 5.-Two
trainmen narrowly escaped death
when two helper" engines plowed
into the rear of Baltimore g. Ohio
Railroad freight train at the tunnel
nesr Mount Airy Junction yesterday
afternoon, wrecking three cars and
badly damaging a locomotive.


The 1$2-car train had just entered
the tunnel east of the junction when
the coupling between the fourth and
fifth cars broke, severing the air hose
and automatically setting the me-
chanical air brakes on the uncoupled
portion Of the train.


The two helper" engines, however,
were proceeded under full steam,
pushing the freight from the rear,
and plowed through three cabooses
as II they were match boxes before
the engineers could cut of their
throttles.


Although the cabooses rose almost
straight into the air and then settled
with a crash on the westbound track,
Conductor Jasper L. HauSe and Flag
man John M. Striegel, both of Balti-
more, who were riding in the second
caboose. escaped unhurt. The front
of the first helper engine was wrecked,
six driving wheels and its pony truck
being derailed and its headlight tossed
so feet away.


One of the cars demolished con-
tanned q consignment of cast iron
pipe being shipped from Holt, Ala.
to the United States Department of
Agriculture's Bureau of Animal Hus-
bandry at Beltsville, Md.


Traffic on the main freight line
was delayed only short time. Sew
eral fast freights bound for New
York were diverted through Mount
Airy. with an abandoned tower at Wa
terville being pressed into service.

ly after midnight, when wrecking
crews from Brunswick completed the
work OF clearing the debris and lift
ing the two deraiied engines back upon
the rails with huge cranes.

WORCESTER, Mass. November
6-Two hundred and fifty Civilian
Conservation Corps workers were
whisked south today despite their re-
bellion against a wholesale transfer
from Maine to Virginia and Maryland
camps.


The youths belabored their officers.
locked them in the baggage car and
thwarted all attempts to move the
12-car troop train for three hours last
night before they were quieted and
the trip was resumed.


A riot call brought $50 policemen
to the yards of the New York. New
Haven g. Hartford Railroad. The ar
rival of police sobered the demon
strators and the Army officers, sew
eral of whom the train conductor said
were beaten badly, asserted they could
take care Of any further trouble.


Worcester police were informed that
discomfort over the transfer had been
brewing since the train left Maine
and that some of the men had been
drinking.


The train arrived in Worcester soon
after 9 pm. for routine stop. After
locking up their officers the youths
held the train by cutting the air hose.


The train. with about a dozen win
dows kicked out departed at 1920
am. for New Haven, Conn, with the
Army officers freed and in control.
The workers are bound for Fort Hoyle,
Md, and Ben Hur, Va.

CHICAGO, June 2.-This long
Spring dry spell, advancing in the
Middle West into It's fourth month,
has one credit mark with meteor
ologists.


Despite the great provocation un-
like past similar periods, it has
brought no noticeable revival Of the
once more or less popular theory that
man ought to be able to make rain.


Reports from over the prairies in
dicate that the glib-talking "profes-
sor" of past droughts, self-designated
rainmaker, has not been sighted COM
ing over the hill to pass the hat
among worry-wracked farmers. He's
apparently extinct.


But these self-styled wizards once
harvested considerable sums from
owners of sun-baked Western fields
laid waste by prolonged dryness.
They popped up in the arid nineties,
impressed a possibly then more SIM
pie folk with their PROFESSIONAL de-
portment and formed numerous rain
making associations to finance their
activities.


Some preached that If the upper
atmospheric reaches could be sufi-
GENTLY jarred-and the professors
palms sufficiently crossed with sill
ver-rain must fall. Big guns were
wheeled through dusty fields and
shots riddled the celestial ceiling.
Dynamite was catapulted into the
sky, bomb kites and balloons were
launched into the air and exploded.


The same methods were tried to
quench forest fires and revive de-
hydrated crops. But usually Jupiter
Pluvius enjoyed a chuckle at the
humor Of it all.


Others Of the rain-making gentry
tried more occult schemes whose
mysteries were known only to them
selves, but who found customers OF
the main highways who would pay
them for their effort.

By MARGARET WlDDEMER
This is the New Year, entering
Our house. Who knows what it may bring?
The times are strange; all this tonight
Of bells and horns and whirling light
May be the drums and flags unfured
Of an unknown, new-builded world.
This world is ours to build again
Behind this door, this window-pane,
For what's world however wide,
But houses with ourselves inside?
If hate break out it's evil fire,
Our hearth can flame its strong love higher,
Teaching the children at our knees
The splendid old integrites
Forging future they control
From WISDOM peace from strength of soul.
For all that we withhold or give
Is chain, or armor, while they live,
And who can rear fortress tall
And strong is the first home wall?
We are the world whose windows light
Our little piece of road tonight
See other windows CLEAN to meet
The steadfast lights along street!

TRENTON, N. j., June 12.-The
New Jersey code authority's action in
fixing tire prices higher than those
under the national rubber code was
declared illegal today by Vice Chal.-
cellor John H. BackeS.


Sears, Roebuck & Co was charged
by State authorities with selling tires
at about 81 less than the prices set
under the State code The company s
prices were in accordance with the
national code, which the concern
claimed took precedence over the
State code.


The jurist ruled. in dismissing the
complaint, that this is national re-
covery, and not merely New Jersey
recovery, and the Governor-or rather
his appointed agents - overstepped
their BOUNDS when they established
prices higher than those approved by
the President"

One hundred billion dollars
worth of gold legislation was
grouped together yesterday by the
United States Supreme Court and
set for hearing on January 8.
This action was taken at the
request of James Crawford Diggs,
the United States Solicitor Gen.
eral.


So important does the Govern
ment consider the litigation that
Attorney General Cummings per-
sonally will argue the cases before
the Supreme Court.


The legislation. passed June S,
1888, set aside the provision in
contracts that payments must be
made in gold.


The suits were based on the
contention that after devaluation
of the dollar payments would be
made in currency worth only
59.06 per cent as much as before.


The Government contends that
the purchasing power Of the cur
rency did not depreciate nearly
that much and that the welfare
of. the many instead of the few
should control.

Seven Forts Are Captured BY Para

ASUNCION, Paraguay, November
II R.-Bolivia's Pilcomayo army col
lapsed today and seven Bolivian forts
fell into Paraguay's hands.


Wild, unrestrained rejoicing swept
this capital as the news spread that
Fort Ballivian, the stout outpost
against which five successive waves of
Paraguayan soldiers had beaten only
to fall back in bloody failure, had
been taken.


Many here were ready to predict
that the two-and-one-half years Of
bitter fighting for possession of the
low, swampy Chaco Boreal was nearly
at an end.


With the shattered remnants Of the
Bolivian forces in the Pilcomayo sec
tor retreating northward along the
only road left open to them-that fol-
lowing the banks of the river-reports
reaching Asuncion said Paraguay had
taken 10000 prisoners in the smash
ing victory, considered the biggest
of the war.


Among the prisoners, those reports
said. were so high ranking officers
ana 500 officers of lesser grade.


The forts that fell with Ballivian
included Guachalla, farther up the
river, which earlier reports indicated
might provide the retreating Bolivians
their second line of defense. Tonight
enemy troops were reported fleeing
In wild disorder toward Villa Monies.
major Bolivian army base.

Armadillos. when fully grown, weigh

are easily tanned and not only make

lovable ones.


Burrows are dug deep into the

Spring rolls around they are pretty
hungry. Insects are hunted industri-
ously from morning till night.


Being socially inclined, you will

as a rule, smiling abou. plowed fields,
pushing over old rotting logs, where

sorst Of places where insects are

In view of the fact that these insect

trude upon mans supplies, II Is

hunt for ground birds eggs and young.

mouth should prove beyond all doubt
this accusation. II is man himself

quail. partridge, woodcock and wild
turkey.


Hundreds of tests have been made
and not one stomach revealed any
thing but insects. The varied diet
consisted OF Rrasshoppers, caterpillars,
cutworms. beetles, spiders, flies, etc.

babies are never permitted 10 90 out

Attracting perhaps the largest
crowd ever to witness such an eXhlbl-
ton in Washington, the unique Cherry
Blossom Festival horse show was held
yesterday afternoon on the Tidal
Basin foot ball grounds before the
festival queen, Miss Eleanor Roosevelt,
her attendants, dignitaries OF the city
and Federal Government and ap-
proximately 5000 spectators.


Horses of all types, breeds and ac-
complishments converged on the show
grounds for the IL events inaugurated
by the coronation of the queen. Fol-
lowing the ceremonies, grand parade
of the equine entrants circled the
field while radio announcers de-
scribed their uses for pleasure, work,
sport and war.


Many Features.


Hunting pink and the drab uni
forms of Cavalry soldiers mixed in
the procession, which was succeeded
by series of show ring classes, ex-
hibition rides and other novel features
arranged by the Horse Show Com
mittee under the direction of Col.
G. L. Scott


Because of threatening skies, the
queen and her court withdrew from
the reviewing stand shortly after the
first ring class was ended.


One of the most spectacular diver
sions of the afternoon was the hunt
teams contest in which pink-coated
riders from the Warrenton, Middle
burg, Washington Riding & Hunt
Club, Redland, Cobbler and Fairfax
hunts competed. A trio from Fort
Myer also entered, winning second
place after the judge had selected
Mrs. Robert c. Winmill's Warrenton
team for top honors. Mrs. Winmill's
entry of Gin Quidado, My Toy and
Renault, was ridden by herself and
her two daughters. Another family
combination, Col. and Mrs. George
Patton, jr, and their daughter, was
third. Handicapped by soggy and
slippery going. several of the riders
encountered near disaster during the
afternoon, but none of them was hurt.


Daring Riding by Troopers.


The brilliant Cossack riding troop
ers of Fort Myers Sd Cavalry went

undeterred by the risky footing.


Thrilled by the reckless horseman-
ship. the crowd applauded briskly as
Army equestrians rode their mounts
from tip to tail. swinging perilously
from saddle horns to the ground, per-
forming hand stands and shoulder
rolls as the horses galloped down the
field.


The enthusiastic audience, a large
percentage of them enjoying first
taste of the show ring, was charmed
by two children's hunt teams. which
appeared in formal pink, black boots
and toppers. The team entered by
Estler Palmer of Bancroft, Va, turned
In the best performance of the after
noon on three brown ponies, taking
the course in excellent form and with
spacing the envy of older riders. That
aggregation, consisting Of Miss Mar
garet Hill, Miss Edna Roth and Bobby
Palmer, won the cup, while the Col
bert trio of Fredericksburg, Va, was
close second on three clever Welsh
hackney ponies.


Foxhounds Shown.


Daniel c. Sands, master of the Mid
dleburg hunt, put on another popu-
lar act when he led into the inclosure
his handsome pack of American fox
hounds, guided by a huntsman and
whip in hunting uniform. Circling
the field in perfect unison and re-
spending with remarkable discipline
to the commands of the huntsman,
the hounds supplied one of the out
standing diversions of the series staged
between each ring contest in order to
eliminate the coStumary lull of the
judging period


Sergt. Alvin T. Moore's dressage
exhibition with a meticulously trained
thoroughbred now being schooled for
the Olympic games also caught the
favor of the crowd, as did the mounted
brass bands galloping tunes.


In the open hunter class which
took the center of the stage after the
draft horses, polo ponies, saddlers
hunters and Army mounts had ended
their parade, Maj George S. Patton
jr., rode his own Wild Ben to victory
and received the cup from Mrs. Henry
Latrobe Roosevelt, mother of the
cherry blossom queen. Tom Cooke
huntSman of the Washington hounds,
rode a good bay from the Frank Bur-
rows Stables to second place, and
Claude Owens Ranger was third.


The Burrow2 string came to the
fore again in the ladies' hunter divi-
sion when Grey Eagle captured the
blue, with Mrs. Winmill's Gin Quidado
second and Maj. Wilfrid Blunt's
entry third.


Assisting Col. Scott in announcing
the information about yesterdays
events was Wayne Dinsmore. well
known Chicago horse expert and
president of the American Horse AS
sociation.

NEW YORK, July 5.-The
Griffs are away from their home
lot again.


Usually this situation means
victories and plenty Of them as in
the past Manager Cronin's gang
has shown itself to better advan.
tage on foreign fields than at
home.


This trip, however. promises to
be more important than any other
taken this season in that the team
must win and win consistently to
get within striking distance Of the
leaders.


Twenty Games Slated


Altogether 20 games are on
schedule. The first bracket fea-
lures a four-game series beginning
here today against the New York
Yankees.


Following this set, Cronin takes
his boys to Detroit, where a
one-day stand will be made
against the Detroit Tigers. Cleve-
land will be visited next for four
games, Detroit again for three
more, st. Louis after that, for
four contests, and Chicago last
for four tiItS. the trip ending
July %.


The toughest bit of the journey
comes right at the start, or while
the Griffs are battling the Yam
KEGS here. In this series, the
Griffs can either make or mar
their chances Of getting back in
the race.


Three Wins Needed


In reality Cronin and his gang
must gather at least three vic.
tories here in order to help not
only themselves but the race gen.
orally. Needless to say, this con-
Stitutes a large order, yet the
boys should fare pretty well, if
their past record on road trips
means anything at all.


When the team came back from
Philadelphia the other night, the
prospects that good pitching might
continue seemed unusually bright.
But today the situation is entirely
changed, due to yesterdays sor-
rowful showing against the Phila-
delphia AS, which found every
Griff hurler in stress.


However, there was still that
chance left today that Manager
Cronin's boys might get back into
winning fettle, once thoughts OF
yesterdays defeats are forgotten,
At least the talent among the staff
is still there, even in the cases of
Gen. Alvin Crowder, Bob Kline,
Bob Burke and Alex McColl all
of whom experienced tough go.
ing" yesterday.


HurlerS Changed


Cronin, incidentally, announced
a change in his pitching plans to.
day for the first two games Of the
current series against the YankS.
For this afternoons opening en-
counter, Lefty" Walter Stewart
was to take the mound. Tomor.
row Earl Whitehill will see service.

NEW YORK, May IA Q.N.SO.
Hitting all sections of the list, a
new concerted selling wave today
sent the stock market tumbling to
new lows for the year, with losses
running as much as six and seven
points in some lines.


The outburst hit its stride
shortly after noon and in the
rush of liquidation rails, motors
and chemicals took the brunt Of
the attack.


Allied chemical was a special
target, breaking more than six
points to its lowest price since
last October. The drive also un'
settled Union Carbide and other
chemical shares.


U. S. Steel and other steel
shares also felt the break. big
steel" sold down more than two
points to a new low for the year.
Sympathetic selling broke out in
Bethlehem, Republic and other
steel stocks.


Trading picked up on the de-
cline, with the ticker falling two
minutes behind.


Motor shares, particularly Gen.
eral Motors and Chrysler, were
sold steadily, and selling in the
rails, notably New York Central,
Southern and Lackawanna, as
Sumed Sizeable proportions.


Commodity markets were weak
in sympathy, and selling in wheat
sent International Harvester down
three points on a small turnover.
Other farm equipment shares
were off.

With flood waters in the
Potomac and other streams in this
section abating today, apprehen-

might cause new floods.


With occasional rains forecast,
the Weather Bureau pointed out

the heavy rains of the past few
days that even light rains would
cause streams to rise.


In the Shenandoah Valley the
highest water in 10 years was re-
corded, with the water "a feet over
the loW-Water mark.

the carrying away of the foot.
bridge from Rosslyn to Roosevelt

Both the Reichstag and the Reichs-
rat whipped Chancellor Adolf Hitler's
monumental reform bill through with
no more outward manifestation than
minor vote of confidence would have
required. There was no debate. The
vote was unanimous.

fiery address marking the first ami

many was plotting against her inde-
pendence.


Discussing the law which shears all
power from German states, once proud
entities OF national life. Minister for
Justice Hans Frank said states were
now mere provinces of the Reich"


State Parliaments have ceased to
exist" he said. Only state councils
appointed by advising with state pre-
miers remain"


The legislation also gave the German
cabinet powers to change the constitu-
ton at will, fact pointed out as illus
trating perfectly the leadership prin-
ciple in actual practice.

NEW YORK, April IA brisk post
Easter retail trade, the resumption OF
wholesale buying, numerous wage in
creases and rising production. steel

labor disturbances, a decline in car

Washington adviceS, indicating that

Wage increases, ranging from 10 to

100000 workers in such varied fields

Also Show Increases.


Electric output, bituminous coal

creaseS. Automobile makers this week

While the sales of women's dresses,

week preceding, particularly in those
districts where adverse weather con-
ditions prevailed. sales of furniture
housewares, electrical refrigerators and
rugs increased by a wide percentage.


Sales of mems and women's wear
ing apparels. however, still are in the

the call for drygoods. Sales of hard
ware, paints, gardening tools and

distancing Spring figures for the last
three years.


while millinery, hosiery, gloves

ings of furniture and housewares, it

heaviest movement was recorded. One

creased earning power of the masses

Stocks Depleted.


The better than expected Easter
trade found many stores with Spring
merchandise unequal to their needs.

orders placed during the week. Mail
orders were especially numerous for
dress accessories, some OF the most
popular sizes of suits. millinery and
handbags. The wholesale market also
reported rush for cotton goods in
anticipation OF national cotton week,
which is scheduled for May IA to 10.


Orders for locomotives in some CEN
ters during March were the largest
for any month in the last three years
and about five times as large as those
booked in March, 1888. Untitled
orders are nearly doubled, reaching
the highest total since March, 1882.
All of which cheered other manufac-
turers of capital goods.


Brisk business at Eastertide natur-
ally sent larger groups of buyers to
primary markets to get merchandise
for April promotions. They found
that the decline in wholesale COM
modify prices had been checked-in
fact, their rise resumed-and wages in
many quarters being advanced. Faced
with depleted stocks and prospects

their selections were made cautiously,
on the theory that public purchasing
power has not expanded sufficiently to
risk stocking merchandise that seems
out of line

ern pact. With peace assured on her

Stanford Day.


CATURDAY was Stanford day from


Franklin Field to Prestwick. 1t


was one of the largest days any
single university ever had in sport.


While Lyman, Dunn, Klofstock,
Blackman and others were showing
what seven men surrounded by 700
rivals could turn out, Lawson Little
was carrying the Cardinal banner at
Prestwick to the top of COLTS tallest
peak.


No one can blame James Wallace.
the carpenter, for finishing with a dull
saw against this Western avalanche.
After beating five Walker cup stars in
a row. he was in no fix to face a
barrage that was 10 under even As,
8 under par, in the final stand. That
was more than Scotland could ask
from William Wallace and Robert
Bruce together


Lawson Little's final blast comes
close to being the greatest single
days performance, considering all
circumstances, that golf ever has
known. Only skill youth, power and
rare emotional inspiration could
have produced such harvest. 1t
was uncanny and the wonder is that
James Wallace didn't rush from the
Prestwick links around the sixteenth
hole and dive into the sea.


Wallace had come forward far be-
vond his earlier dreams and hopes.
He carried the dreams and hopes OF
Scotland. He knew this, and it made
the burden no lighter. And then he
suddenly was called on to face a
murderous fusillade of brides and
pars. a blast strong enough to wreck
any two men, much less worn and
lone survivor A marvellous short
game touch hooked itself to Little's
power. and the result was a golfing
miracle.


The Stanford entry will have his
share of the big gallery at Merton
just 10 days away.


Meanwhile, Stanford's seven men at
Franklin Field, ably backed by Cali
fornia's still smaller team, proved
again how far Western supremacy
has left the East behind. Five of her
men could have won without strain
ing any ligaments. And this takes
nothing from the great running of
Bill Bonthron.

BUENOS AIRES, December pa
Christmas truce in the Chaco Boreal
appeared little likely today as Para
quay made ready to hurl thousands
of picked troops against Bolivia's last
line defenses in what observers said
might be the decisive battle of the
war.


From all directions Paraguayan col
unlns were closing in on Villa Monies,
Bolivias central army base, and the
La Paz government maSsed all avail
able reserves in that sector, asserting
its defenses were impregnable.


Meanwhile advices from Asuncion
said official circles doubted the feasi-
bility of any truce such as that sug-
gested by the Vatican, pointing out
that both armies were spread over
such wide fronts that the armistice
would be tactically impractical.


La PaZ reported Gen. Jose Estigar-
ribia, Paraguayan commander in chief,
was preparing to strike at Villa Mon
tes, while Asuncion reports said Bo-
livia was massing men and munitions
in several sectors apparently making
ready for an impending counter-ofen
sive.


With minor skirmishes reported in
three sectors, three Paraguayan col
umns, each comprising one entire
army corps, moved toward Villa
Monies.

ANNAPOLIS. September 19.-Dick
Pratt, Washington MILDLY, appears to
have won his fight, for the time at
least, for the quarterback position
on the Naval Academy varsity team.
He has been waging keen fight
in a field of several aspiran.S, and
his strongest competitor is Holey Lee.
Both youths had some experience in
the position last year and the battle
between the two is so close that either
finally may hold the job though just
now Pratt is leading. The others IN
the backfield in the tentative lineup
just determined upon are Buzz Berries,
halfback: Bill Clark, fullback, both
regulars last year. and Tommy King,
a change back last year. who is ahead
of the field for the other halfback
positions.


The veterans probably will be picked
in the line, for the opening game
at least, though in every case they
will have a stiff fight to hold on
against the younger players. Capt.
Dick Burns and Dave Zabriskie,
guards, and Slade Cutter and George
Lambert, tackles, were regulars last
season, and Bob Dornin and Bob
Mandelkorn were change ends. Lou
Robertshaw was Bob Harbold's under
study and did a lot of match playing.
Both line and backfield average less
than last year.

more than 70 persons in an emerg-

shrieks of the $500 frantic in
mates. Doctors and nurses from

buildings and uprooting trees.

NEW ORLEANS, August 25-Plain
citizens who have stood between the
armed political camps of Huey p.
Long and Mayor T. Semmes Walmsley
for more than a north, today decided

Banking themselves into deter

narily take no prominent part in
politics, called on their fellow citizens

derly procedure at the polls when the
Long and Walmsley factions go to the
mat in the congressional primary
September II.

mented and heavily armed, continued

would start its investigation into the
city administration remained in doubt,
although Long freely expressed favor

threatened with impending bank
ruptcy.

and our loans from the banks are

LOS ANGELES, Dec. 6 GN.S).
Death today was revealed as stalk
ing the modern Eden of the Paci-
fic on Charles Island, of the mys-
teriouS and little-known Galapagos
group. Radio messages from Capt.
G. Allen Hancock, Los Angeles
scientist-explorer, received at his
offices here, from the cruiser
Velero III, on which Captain Han
cock is taking party of Smith
sonian Institution scientists to the
island, solved the mystery of the
death Of two men on lonely Mar
chena Island of the Galapagos.


The radio also announced the
death of DR.. Frederick Ritter, Ger
man scientist who went into a
self-imposed exile on the islands
with his common-law wife, Frau
Dore Strouch Koerwein.


At the same time it was re-
vealed Baroness BoSquet Won Wag-
ner, self.termed empress of the
island, and her friend, Robert
Phillipson, have been missing
from the islands for more than
five months and are believed to
have perished.


Identifies Bodies


Captain Hancock, forsaking his
beloved science long enough to
turn detective, definitely identified
the bodies found on Marchena
Island some weeks ago as those
of Alfred Rudolph Lorenz, once
close friend of the baroness, who
accompanied her to the islands,
and Trygve Nuggeruud, Norwe-
gian sailor.


With Lorenz and Nuggeruud per-
ished a native, is the belief Of
Capt. Hancock, although the body
was never found.


Residents of the islands, Arthur
Wittmer and his wife and two
children, and Frau Koerwein, told
the dramatic tale of the tragedy
of the Galapagos to the scientists.


These five, the only survivors Of
the little colony on Charles Island,
told Captain Hancock how the bar
onesS, had driven Lorenz from the
island in an open boat without
food or water, on July S.


Tried For Mainland


Lorenz later picked up Mug
geruud and the native boy and
set out for Chatham Island in the
hope of reaching the mainland
from there.


Twenty-one days later an aban-
doned boat of the trio was sighted
from Charles Island, the radio
message declared.


Shortly after driving out
Lorenz, the Baroness and Phillip
son departed from the islands.
No trace of them has been found
since that time.


PRESIDENT of the islands told
Captain Hancock, who had visited
Marchena and identified the
mummified bodies of Lorenz and
Nuggeruud before coming here,
that the trio apparently had been
dashed on Marchena's rocky
shores by a storm, one of their
boats being wrecked and the
other swept away.

defending himself by stating that

homes, and that practically all
had been travelling in bad company
and had been arrested at one time
or another before they came under
his control.


Charges against Cannon were
filed by Merle Trader, brother OF

From the Atlanta Constitution.


Georgia's most fortunate cotton
growers-those who have produced
the most cotton per acre, received the
best price for their staple and enjoyed
the best demand for their product
held their annual barbecue Thursday
ct Orchard Hill, in Spalding County.


These producers occupy their IA
vored position because they have fol-
lowed up-to-date methods in the pro-
duction of cotton. Banding together
in 1881 to organize the Orchard Hill
Cotton Improvement Association, its
several hundred members pledged
themselves TO plant variety cotton
and to endeayor to increase the yield
per acre.


The result has been increased prof
its from their farming operations and
a bigger demand for their cotton than
they could meet, practically their en-
tire production being bought by Geor-
gia mills engaged in the manufacture
of automobile tires.


The cost of production per acre has
been slightly increased but the mar
gin Of profit has been doubled and
trebled. Their experience has conclu-
sively demonstrated the wisdom Of the
doctrine preached for many years by
Federal and State agricultural experts
that the better the cotton the larger
and more certain the profits will be.
The day when the farmer who
raises cotton on the old hit-or-miss
plan can be prosperous is definitely
over. When the South. was the only
section in the world producing cotton
in any material volume it was pos
sible for Southern growers to plant
any kind of seed, use little or no fer
tilizer and follow old-fashioned meth
ods of cultivation. The result was 9
poor quality Of short-staple cotton.
Now cotton of that kind is being
produced in large volume in Europe
Asia and Africa.

EDMONTON, Alberta, September
28.-Four boys and a girl today were
in the children's shelter here after
their mother, unable to see them con-
tinue with the hardships of a back
woods life, drove them so miles to
Rimbey, and turned them over to the
Alberta Neglected Children's Depart
Uent.


They were brought to Edmonton by
Royal Canadian Police. When the
children arrived with their mother at
Rimbey they were clothed in flour
sacks and gunny sacking. They had
travelled two days through rain and
snowstorms on small rig drawn by
one horse.


Throughout the Summer the chill
dren played about with little cloth
ing. They have slight colds, but
otherwise their condition is about
normal


The boys are 10, 6, 4 and 8 years
old and the girl, 8. The eldest boy
told officials that all of the children,
including himself, were born in the
backwoods home and that a doctor
had never been in the house
/ The boy said their home has been
a one-room shack, with thin board
roof and a mud floor They have
been eating rabbits, he said. The
mother turned back to the backwoods
homestead.

BY the Associated Press.


LOS ANGELES, September 28.-
Mysteriously trapped by flames, Melvin
Hall, 43, wealthy real estate man, who
married two of his three wives twice,
was burned to death yesterday.


At the time of the fire, his latest
wife, Virginia Hobbs Hall, beauty con-
test winner from Memphis, Tenn, one
of the two he married twice. was
visiting her mother for the night.


Hall was trapped despite efforts Of
his 70-year-old father and several
neighbors to save him. His charred
body was recovered from the ruins of
the Office building Of the Verdugo
Woodlands estate, Is miles northeast
of here


Hall Married Vera May Hays in
1912. After IL years, during which
he amassed a fortune in the real
estate boom, she divorced him on
charges that he was associating with
Elizabeth Roclair The latter and
Hall we're married in 1926 and divorced
two years later.


Then Virginia Hobbs, who held the
title, Miss Memphis" came to Holly
wood and met Hall on blind date. -
Romance followed and they were mar
ried in Mexico in 1929. Mrs. Eliza
beth Hall, however, rewon Halls af-
fections, and he later obtained a Mex
ican divorce from the beauty winner
and married his second wife again.


But Virginia Hall entered the pic
ture again and in a few months Hall
was sued for separate maintenance by
Elizabeth Hall. The real estate man
countered with a suit asking that his
second marriage to Elizabeth be an
nulled on grounds that his Mexican
divorce from Virginia was not legal.
He said he had gone back to Virginia
and wanted to resume legal marital
status with her, but found himself
with two wives.


Investigating the fire, deputy sheriffs
said there were indications Hall had
struggled with some one else or had
fought desperately to escape the
flames before being overcome. A
heavy lounge was found overturned,
the deputies said. Last night. how
ever, tbe officers said they had found
no evidence indicating the fire was set
by some one else.

neyS of flame.

building was an old brick Struc.
ture, for many years a favorite

lieved among the dead. He was
not seen after he plunged into
the smoke-filled lobby in an eff.

BY the Associated Press.


Negotiations for a settlement of
Soviet-American debts and claims,
which collapsed two weeks ago when
the United States rejected Russian
demand for long-term credits and a
loan as its price" to pay American
claims, were reopened today at the
State Department.


Alexander Troyanovsky, the Russian
Ambassador. resumed the discussions
with Secretary Hull and Assistant Sec.
retary Moore.


The American claims, under the
Soviet proposal, would be paid from
a fund made up from extra interest
charges on all Soviet purchases made
through the export bank with Amer
ican credits.


The United States was understood
to have been willing to grant the
Soviet credits, but flatly rejected the
request for a cash loan.


Neither the State Department nor
Troyanovsky had any statement to
make when the conference began.

for the identity of the person who
set the fires, but they met with little
success.

several other small ones which police
believe had some connection with the
major one.

BY the Associated Press.


It's Mrs. Franklin D. RooSevelt's
50th birthday anniversary today, but
Sistie and Buzzie Dali are much more
excited over it than is the First Lady.


So that the grandchildren might
blow out the birthday candles, the
celebration was fixed for tea-time
instead of dinner. And the cake was
about all the feStivity Mrs. Roosevelt
would permit. for her theory is:


The more you forget your birth
day anniversary as you grow older,
the younger you stay"


Mrs. James Roosevelt, mother Of
the President, who celebrated her
80th birthday anniversary at a Hyde
Park party a few weeks ago, was ex-
pected for tea.


Mr.. and Mrs. Elliott Roosevelt, who
live nearby in Virginia, planned to
drop in. Elliott said:


Mothers dificult person to cele-
brate birthdays with. She wants the
day to slide over with as little fuss
as possible


Mrs. Roosevelts daily calendar was
peculiarly clear Of public appearances
for the day-perhaps because she
didn't wish the public to make a fuss
over it either.


But the First Ladys friends remem-
bered the date. Flowers filled every
vase, kilograms stacked up, gifts and
good wishes poured into the White
House


1t has long since become an axiom
that Anna Eleanor Roosevelt is the
most widely acquainted mistress the
White House ever had. In her year
and a half there she has Travelled
more miles, taken part in more social
welfare and educational movements,
come into closer contact with more
people in a dozen ways than any pre-
vious First Lady.


Cutting through tradition, she has
given interviews to the press, talked
over the radio and made surprise visits
to the Natior's sore spots" She has
given impetus to many Federal moves
in behalf Of women and children
nursery schools, child-feeding pro-
grams, camps for unemployed. unat-
tached women. and projects for the
lost generation" of high school and
college graduates who couldn't get
jobs.


She has invited, received and
answered a prodigious mail, mostly
heart -pourings from persons In dire
economic straits Many of them she
has been able to help.


And in all these ways she has made
personal acquaintances, the kind that
prompted today's happy birthday to
you, Mrs. Roosevelt"

NEW YORK, May 26.-The Stock
Market continued its creeping prog
ress today and a number of issues
recorded relatively substantial gains
in subnormal activity. Although SEN
timent was noticably improved,
traders were still cautious and public
participation was at a minimum The
close was steady, and the turnover
approximated only 100000 shares.


The improved tone displayed by
equities was attributed partly to a
slightly brighter brand of Washington
developments and scattered indications
that business and industry are begin
ming to show resistance to the season
letdown.


Grains Go Higher.


Just how much encouragement
stocks received from the forward move
ment of grains was matter of argu-
ment. Cash corn sold at so cents a
bushel, the highest since July last year.
Wheat got up more than a cent
bushel, but yielded most of its advance
upon profit-taking based on forecasts
of unsettled weather in the North
west.


Silver and rubber futures were
about even. Followers of the white
metal were not especially enthusiastic
over the administrations demands for
so per cent profits tax. Cotton did
better. Bonds we're a little ragged,
although United States Governments
securities scored further small gains.
The dollar was again higher in terms
of leading foreign exchanges.


American Sugar Refining shares got
up 2, as did those of Allied Chemical.
Others fractionally to around a point
higher included American Telephone,
United States Steel, Case, Interna-
tional Harvester, Borden. Chrysler,
Sears Roebuck, Montgomery Ward,
Santa Fe, Howe Sound, Cerro de
Pasco, American Tobacco B. Lggett
g. Myers B. Reynolds B. Schenley,
United States Industrial Alcohol.
Great Western Sugar. United Aircraft
and American Smelling. The motors
and utilities did little.


Leaders Pare Gains.
Most of the leaders pared their
gains in the final half hour and some
even finished with slight losses. There
was a brief furry in the sugar group
on announcement of new beet sugar
quotas and expectation that insular
quotas would be given out next week.
The street felt little better about
the Stock Exchange control bill fol-
lowing reports from Washington that
. the President, in order to expedite
passage of the measure, had agreed to
the Glass provision for special regu-
latory commission. The Chief Execu-
tive had previously approved the
House bill which would have placed
regulation in the hands of the Federal
Trade Commission. Brokerage houses
believe they can get along easier with
a separate body in control.
While threats of even more serious
labor troubles were not being over
looked, hopes were expressed that the
Government would be able to success
fully mediate the more pressing con-
troversies.

ping and growing WEAKNESS.


During daily returns to conscious
ness. which are growing shorter. the
62-year- -old actress hears read to her
the letters which have poured in
from countless friends and admirers
over the world.


Few Friends Admitted.


Allen Breed Walker, resort owner,
and Mrs. Walker, close friends of the
actress, are the only ones now ad-
mitted to the sick room in the home
on the estate of c. K. G.. Billings.


The Walkers, who have not left
the estate since Miss Dressler ex-
pressed the desire to come here
three months ago when the inroads
of cancer and uremic poisoning
forced her to stop her film work,
have been forced to bring their secre-
tary here to care for the mail.


All the letters are opened and
Walker reads them to Miss Dressler
as long as she is able to listen.


Elsie Janis, Mary Pickford, Irving
Thalberg, Margaret Mayo, Amos and
Andy. President and Mrs. Roosevelt
and many others have sent their
good wishes.


Miss Dressler's bravery has never
wavered during the long and hope
less fight.


Patient Without Pain.


The actress has felt no pain from
the time about three weeks ago when
her sickness took a more serious
turn.


To the question Of her head nurse,
Lila Farris, "are you comfortable,
dear?" Miss Dressler always has an
swered yes"


Although only a ghost of smile
now comes to her face, Miss Dressler
acknowledges her friends with her
eyes, they say.


In constant attendance is Mamie
Cox colored, personal maid Of the
actress for the last Is years. Push
ing aside the expert kitchen staff of
the estate, Mamie prepares the food
she knows her mistress likes.


The bed on which the actress
awaits the end has been so arranged
that she. can look over pond Of

A public meeting tonight at the
Jewish Community Center will bring
together representatives of the va
rious local organizations interested
in the United Jewish Campaign.


The meeting will officially launch
the $35,000 drive for relief of desti-
tute Jews Of Europe and for Pales-
tine rehabilitation. Among the speak

estinian labor leader, and Joeph c.
Hyman, secretary of the American
Joint Distribution Committee, largest
international Jewish relief agency.

Hershfleld and Edmund I. Kaufman,
co-chairmen Of the drive, and DR..
Abram Simon, honorary chairman.


The local drive Is part of a ma
tional united Jewish appeal, designed
to raise 100000 throughout the
United States this year for relief work
abroad.


The Council Of Jewish Women, the
Hadassah, the District Zionist organi-
zation and other local Jewish organi-
cations are busy organizing drive di-
visions. The Mizrachi Society, meet

munity Center, approved the choice

campaign.

Police investigating the Staying of 13-

three men for questioning today un-
der high bond on vagrancy charges.


One was Gilbert Jacobs, 81, for

Dillon, worked as houSekeeper.
Detectives said they were told a rifle

William Jackson, 80, and Addison
jackson, 20. brothers. The Jacksons,
police said, were arrested and con-
yicted last February 81 on charge
of molesting children at the Shelby
Street Bridge under which the Dillon
boys body was found.


As detectives planned to question
the men, the mother, who tainted as

home from the shock.


Donald. described as a studious,
book-loving boy who was to have
entered high school Monday, disap-
peared Sunday night. Not until a
rainstorm yesterday did the body,
stuffed into the sewer, float out into
view of three workmen who had taken
refuge under the bridge.


Oflcers sought for questioning two
men, each about 80, who made in
quiries concerning Donald at a nearby
tire shop Sunday night, q few hours
after he had left home.


Donald's father, Shirley Dillon,
from whom his mother has been di-

days.

where Henriette married Louis
Dannenbaum, a prominent silk
merchant. They lived here dur
ing the Lincoln administration,
and Mrs. Dannenbaum remember
ed many incidents of the life of
the President during the Civil
War.


Later they moved to Philadel-
phia.

BOISE, Idaho, April 30.-The devas-
tating Mormon" crickets, which came
into prominence in 1348 when they
threatened first colonists in Utah with
starvation, have appeared in a half
dozen spots of Southern Idaho to
carry on the destruction they started
last year.


Huge black creatures two inches
long when tuil grown, they eat every
thing in sight, including their own
young or injured. When banded to-
gether they have mastered almost
every device set up against them
except tin fences and poison dust.


Packed into almost solid phalanxes,
they move toward cultivated fields and
their eating sounds like wind blowing
constantly among the leaves.


Desperate Mormon settlers, from
whose experience with them the in
sects get their name, tried every de-
vice available, but lacked poison or
tin in sufficient quantities. The
Latter Day Saints history credits sea
gulls from islands in the great Salt
Lake with saving them from starva-
ton.


The sea gulls, swarmed in by
thousands. gorged on the crickets and
carried them to water courses or to
the salty lake, and there disgorged
them. A monument near the Salt
Lake Temple now ccmmrmorates the
event.

LONDON, October 22.-The deflni-
ton of the term defensive arma-
ments" already threatened today as
a barrier to easy agreement in the
naval conversations opening tomor-

Britain.
