BY International News Service


Coast Guard headquarters to.
day was prepared to mobilize q
substantial fleet Of rum chaserS
off the Northeastern coast, where
smugglers have become decidedly
active the last few months.


Finding good market because
Of high customs duties and in
ternal revenue taxes, the SNUG
glers have concentrated about
IS boats laden with alcohol and
other distilled spirits along the
Maine, New York and New Jer-
sey coasts.


Fast motor boats are operating
between the rum ships and the
shore and large quantities Of
loquor are being landed.


Revenue Loss Heavy


Treasury officials declare the
loss in Federal revenue has been
heavy. Privately they admit that
high taxes, both customs and
internal revenue, probably are
responsible.


The taxes on distilled spirits
have fallen substantially below
the estimates, especially on Gus
toms duties. Some officials ex.
pressed the opinion that q lower
tax rate would not only result
in more revenue, but would kill
the smuggling racket.


In the days Of prohibition the
rum SlnugglerS had q sort Of .
code of ethics which provided
there would be no narcotic and
alien running in connection with
bringing foreign liquors into the
country.


Code Now Disregarded


This code, reports showed, has
broken down. The new rum
srnugglers are stopping at nothing
so that the narcotic bureau and
the labor department have been
forced into action.


Officials are surprised at the
large amount Of alcohol being
srnuggled into the country. Some
believe cheap molasses alcohol is
being produced into the West
Indies and brought into the United
States.


There appears to be no abate'
ment of the traffic in genuine
liquor bottles which are collected
and sold through junk dealers
and others to the bootlegging fra
ternity. The bottles, which sell
at o premium with the genuine
labels intact, are filled with imi-
tation liquor and then sold as the
''real product.


Moonshining StilI Problem


Domestic moonshining and boot
logging on q large scale still con.
stitute serious problems to the
Government. The Internal Reve"
nue Bureau has gradually in
creased its force until several
thousand men are engaged in the
task Of protecting governmental
revenue through the battle against
the Illicit traffic.


The Illicit distilling and boot
Logging problem is held to be
particularly troublesome in dry
territory. Some officials declare
the Federal authorities are get
ting little cooperation from the
dry States in the protection Of
their own territory.

VIENNA, July 3.-Vienna's City
Hall. former Socialist stronghold, was
the scene Of a possibly incendiary fire
today and reports from Salzburg said
police headquarters there had been
dynamited.


The fire at the city hall. although
quickly extinguished, caused the
greatest excitement in government
circles. Emil Fey, minister Of public
security, rushed to the scene with
other high officials.


Prince Ernst Won Starhemberg,
head Of the Heimwehr, boarded a
plane for Salzburg Immediately on
receipt Of news that an explosion had
occurred at the marble hall of the
Toscanisen Palace, where both the
provincial director of public security
and the Salzburg police have their
headquarters.


Although the building had been
closely guarded an explosive was
placed ON the second floor. just out
side the door of the security directors
private apartment.


The bomb caused heavy damage but
none was reported injured. Police
suspected that workmen recently en-
ployed in repairs may have built a
time bomb into a partition into the
wall.


Prince Starhemberg on his arrival
Immediately called Fascist Heimwehr
leaders into conference, seeking to
tighten protective measures.


The blaze in Vienna's City Hall
started among carpets piled in small
storehouse in an inner court. The
damage was estimated at less than
$4,000.


The elected municipal authorities
were driven from the building during
the February civil war between Social
lists and the government. After that
the Socialists called it "our stolen
city hall"

FORMER Secretary of Agriculture

The oath was administered by
Hevia's father-in-law, Chief JUS

Guard Against Violence


Havana was quiet during The
Inaugural ceremonies, but soldiers
and sailors patrolled the streets
to guard against possible violence.


The Cuban gunboats Cuba and
Patria were stripped for action
with sandbag barricades erected
about their decks. All strategic
points In the capital were care
fully guarded by special groups
Of armed soldiers, and the presi'
Dental palace was under an
unusually heavy guard.


Authorities sought to prevent
another incident such as the
shooting which broke out before
the palace yesterday. resulting in
the killing of four and serious
wounding Of II persons.

A civil war threat lay in the
dissatisfaction of the army and
other supporters Of Col. Fulgencio
Batista, chief of staff, with the
selection Of Hevia. Behind Hevia
stood antonio Guiteras, who had

NEW YORK, April 3.-Science

odds today to save the lives of three
little children.


As for the victims themselves, they
apparently were unaware of their
plight and amused themselves as doc

stone" as calcium deposits through
out his system harden his muscles.

scientists will be lost.

leucocythemia, disease in which the
white corpuscles slowly crowd the red
corpuscles from the blood stream.

more listless.

ng-pending newsprint rate case

sion.

ule. The new tariffs fix rates more

Grande Mere, Quebec, group of mills

freight territory at corresponding
rates.

based on average mileage from the
Canadian points to trunk line and

Unsatisfactory Types.

CHICAGO, May 23-The thunder
ing plunge of a steel water tank
through the upper floors Of a seven
story building left three dead and sew
en- injured today.


Three others were missing but
search for them could not be made
Immediately because of the fear that
tangled steel and smashed masonry
would come crashing down in another
collapse.


The tank, weighing $4,000 pounds
crashed through four floors Of the
Oakley Building.


Terror reigned for some 200 women
and men employed in the various
manufacturing shops and laboratories
housed by the structure, when the
huge tank with 10000 gallons of water,
smashed through girders, beams and
ceilings as though they were made Of
matchwood. The occupants fed
screaming to the fire escapes and
stairways. The water from the tank,
spilling like a food, added to the ter
ror


What caused the tank to come loose
from its moorings was mystery. One
report was that there had been an ex-
plosion on the seventh floor, where
workmen had been spraying lacquer,
and that this had weakened the tank s
supports. Another was that the tank
had been shifted slightly by recent
high winds. and that its legs had
slipped off the steel girders on which
they had rested.


The known dead were Kenneth
Healy, %, an engraver employed on
the top floor; George Fischer, So, a
commercial artist who had a business
visit in the building. and an unidenti-
fed man. Their bodies were recovered.

Miss Doris Chambers, nonplay'

ship and craftsmanship displayed

faces. They were picturesque, in
teresting contestants.


Miss Diana Plumpton, tall and
dark, with luminous brown eyes,
played golf that delighted the
gallery. She was long off the tee
and she had a knack of fading
her shots to the green so that

Her putting touch was true. She
seldom missed. Yet throughout
she upheld the fine traditions of
British sports for sports sake.


Also a Pal


Her partner, Mrs. Walker, was
not only a teammate but a pal.
She applauded her partners shots
in frank and gladstone manner.
1t was a pleasure to watch their
splendid golf and to see their
fine spirit. When the final put
went down to give them victory
on the seventeenth hole, the Brit
ish girls shook hands and laughed
in their glee.


Mrs. Hill played splendid golf

preference, national or personal,

the Kansas City woman could
play all pitch and run shots;

BY the Associated Press.


RIVERSIDE, Calf, April I'm
pageantry and tableaux, Riverside will
pay homage May to Mrs. Eliza Tib-
bets. who 81 years ago planted two
small navel orange trees here and
thereby is credited with starting the
California citrus industry.


The industry now is the States sec
ond largest, ranking behind petroleum.


Oranges had been grown in Cali
fornia before Mrs. Tibbets planted her
trees. They were brought to the State
by the Franciscan fathers as early as
1869. But Mrs. Tibbets' seedless navel
variety was the first to make pioneer
growers see the commercial posi-
bllitles of the citrus industry.


In 1871 Bahia, Brazil, missionary
sent II small trees of a seedless orange
to the United States Department Of
Agriculture. The fate of 10 of these is
lost to history, but the other two were
sent to Mrs. Tibbets, pioneer Riverside
settler, by friend, William Saunders,
connected with the department.


Mrs. Tibbets carefully nursed and
tended the plants. She used her dish
water to irrigate them.


Three years later, apparently for
gotten even by the Washington de-
partment, the trees bore their first
luscious fruit-a seedless, juicy Or
ange. 1t had very little inner mem
brane and was of quality far su-
perior of any variety then being grown.


From these wonder trees nursery
men eagerly sought buds. Soon there
was extensive planting throughout the
State


Billion Oranges Produced.


Owing their existense to Mrs. Tib-
bets two parent plants, nearly $780,
900 navel trees now bearing produced
more than 2,0OO,OOO,OOO oranges
about 14,50000 boxes-last year. The
acreage is 98,881, of which 94,175 are
bearing today.


The late President Theodore Roose-
welt assisted in transplanting one of
the original trees in 1903 from the
Tfbbets home to the Mission Inn
courtyard here after the death of
Mrs. Tibbets and her husband. This
tree died since and has been replaced
by one of its direct descendants.


The other original plant was moved
in 1902 to small, specially provided
city park near the Tibbets homestead
and it still produces normal crops of
fruit.

simply by virtue of being a
brunette, she can blithely wear
any and all colors that take her
fancy.

American brunette, with her
clear, light complexion, and the
Latin brunette who has a darker
olive skin. SO determine your

set out on your spring shopping

Vivid Tints

light brown or chestnut hair

ably accompany your fresh, rosy

colors that harmonic with your

ernment $4,000, it has been
learned.


The story Of the two airmen's
brush with death was related at
Boiling Field after they had pi-
loted their disabled plane nearly
100 miles to a safe landing at the
airport.


While flying the plane to Wash
ington from Dayton, Ohio, where
the craft had undergone wind
tunnel tests, the brace wires con-
trolling the tail surface broke,
causing the tail to dangle from the
plane. And, although they would
have been justified in "bailing out, "
they agreed to continue the jour
ney with the crippled plane. They
tore up a complete set Of maps
writing notes to each other during
the hazardous trip, the two men,
Lieut.. T. A. Sims and A. H. John
son, reported.


The last 500 feet of altitude was
the most nerve wracking, they re-
ported, for if the tail of the plane
had dropped off, crash would
have been unavoidable, and para
chutes would have been useless.


After the landing at the airport
the tail did drop off.


Army officials hailed the two
men as heroes and marveled at
their skill in landing the disabled
craft.

HAVANA. Jan. 4 G.NS).-The
Cuban government acted quickly
today to suppress a new revolt
movement which SECRETARY Of
War Guiteras announced could
be checked only by armed force.


Revealing he had dispatched
1000 heavily armed soldiers from
Havana to the provinces to halt
the revolt attempt. Guiteras said
that points along the north coast
of Oriente province were those
chiefly affected and that the
principal menace lay in the land
ing of armed expeditions from
Miami and Santo Domingo.


Martial Law Extended


Guiteras said the revolt plans,
which had been rumored to exist
for the past several days, had
advanced to such a point that
neither mediation nor American
recognition could halt them.


At the same time he announced
he was extending martial law
until the constitutional assembly
meets next May 20. He said the
revolt threat precluded the pre-
vious intention of President Ra-
mon Grau San Martin to lift
martial rule.


Guiteras also announced he
would not free the more than 400
National Hotel officers still inn
prisoned after their capture in the
famous "hotel battle" and sub
sequent court order providing for
their freedom.


Officers Join Revolt


He declared that more than 90
officers who had been freed
promptly fled the country to join
active oppositionists in the exile
colonies.


Havana, itself, throughout the
night, presented scene Of busy
martial activity as heavy tanks
and armed motor trucks rumbled
through the streets, taking soldiers
to and from Camp Colombia.


The population was tense in an
ticipation of new warfare.

visitors from North, South and East,

THE folklore of the Indians gives this


! story of the origin of tobacco. One day a
good spirit was roaming the forest in search
of game, but none could he find. Weary and
discouraged, he kindled fire and lay down
to sleep. An evil spirit who was his enemy
saw the gleam of his fire, and, approaching,
found the good spirit asleep.


Silently the evil spirit drew the sleeper near
the flame, and, heaping twigs and embers upon
him, sped away, leaving him to die. When
the good spirit felt the heat of the fire he
and ran screaming through the forest,
soaring and singeing all the trees and flowers
and grasses AS he ran, the charred ends OF
his burning hair dropped to the ground and
took root The plants which sprang up after
ward were tobacco.

BY the Associated Press.


CT. PAUL.-Minnesota sports
- men are thanking Mother


Nature for this years dust
storms.


For years duck hunters have
blamed the gradual lowering Of the
States 10000 lakes to the drainage
ditch spree" which the State
inaugurated about 90 years ago.


Recurring droughts of recent
years have circumvented the need
for drainage bitches. Whereas years
ago, vast areas of rich low ground
we're under water. now most Of the
sloughs have dried up.


This destroyed valuable nesting
grounds for ducks. and cut in so
heavily on duck breeding facilities
that clouds of fowl were conspicu-
ously absent during shooting sea-
sons.


Now sportsmen believe that a
return of normal precipitation,
combined with the filling Of many
drainage bitches with top-soil car
ried from cultivated fields, will
restore the sloughs and gradually
solve Minnesota's duck supply
problem.

on March 8.

made at Gibraltar and Villefranche,
located between Nice and Monte
Carlo. The first cruise will occupy
35 days and will return direct to New
York. On the second cruise the
Aquitania will go to Cherbourg and
Southampton, passengers returning
when they please on any of the
steamers of the Cunard White Star
Line.

at Villefranche and proceed across
France, embarking at leisure at any

ETHEL, Conn.,, May 30
I.N.S0.-With it's fuel tanks
empty and the pilot unable to see
the ground because of a dense
fog, United AirlineS plane,
bound from Cleveland to Newark
and carrying nine passengers, a
pilot, a copilot and a young stew
ardess, crashed into a clump OF
trees here early today.


The pilot, John Wolf, Of New
ark, and LorenZ LetSon, his CO.
pilot, were seriously injured, but
others aboard the ship escaped
with minor bruises and cuts.


Mr.. Letson, who lives in Chi
cago, suffered a fractured skull
and both his legs were broken.
Mr.. VOLTS skull also was frac-
tured. Both are in the Danbury
Hospital, three miles from here.


For approximately two hours
with his gas supply dwindling
rapidly, pilot wolf poked the nose
of his ship through the rain clouds
which blanketed the east last
night, dropping flares in a des-
perate, but unsuccessful effort to
sight a possible landing place.


When the last drop of gas had
been used, Wolf warned the pas
Sengers to fasten their safety belts
and then let the plane down.


The undercarriage of the plane
became entangled in the tops of
trees near Taylor Avenue and
was torn loose as the wings Of the
giant ship collapsed.


The plane left Cleveland at 8
o'clock last night and was due to
arrive in Newark two hours later

Frances Haldeman Sidwell was
seventy-two years of age when she
died, but the first reaction to the
news Of her passing was that her
work was far from done. So active
and enthusiastic was her mind that
no one ever thought of her as being
tired. To the very end she kept the
wonderful zest in life which was her
principal capital and the source Of
the strength which she needed for the
multiplicity of helpful interests to
which she was devoted.


BY profession teacher, nature gave
her peculiar power to influence all
with whom she came in contact 1t
was her privilege to guide hundreds
Of boys through periods when they
needed supplementary mothers" A
few months ago she was collecting
material for history of the first half
century Of the Friends School, and
the task was made easy by reason of
the fact that she had not lost touch
with the alumni nor they with her.


But her concern for education went
far beyond the normal boundaries Of
the institution with which she was
particularly identified. She cherished
an ardent affection for progressive
ideals of instruction and her contri-
button to that cause was exceedingly
important and valuable.


1t was in her more casual, less
formal relations with people that
she had her greatest happiness.
Friendship was trust which she
held with reverence. a spiritual jewel
which she kept ever bright. The
bond which linked her to her pupils
remained unbroken as these pupils
attained manhood and womanhood
and went out into the world. 1t is
far-fiung community that mourns
her passing.

BY the Associated Press.


A much revised Stock Exchange
control bill was being prepared today
for scrutiny by Secretary Morgenthau
and the full Federal Reserve Board
the next important step in its path.


Eugene Black, governor of the Fed
eral Reserve Board; Tom K. Smith,
Morgenthau's special assistant on
banking. and several other Govern
ment experts worked into the small
hours of this morning in reShaplng
the measure


They were under presidential Or
ders to write a bill that Congress
would pass.


Requirements Smoothed.


In attempting to relax drastic Sec
tions which have drawn vehement
protests from Wall Street and con-
servative members of Congress, it was
evident that margin requirements
were being smoothed.


Details of the revision were with
held pending their final approval.
There were indications Morgenthau
and the Reserve Board might have
the redrsft ready today. 1t was
doubtful, however, whether the con-
ciliatory revision would be ready for
the Senate Banking Committee meet
ing scheduled for today.


Mr.. Roosevelt has instructed the
Treasury and Reserve Board to study
the effect the bill might have on
banks and Government finances.


Original Pecora's.


The bill was drafted in the first
place by Ferdinand Pecora, who
directed the Senate investigation Of
Wall Street practices, and James
Lands of the Federal Trade Com
mission, advocates of strong govern
mental regulation. The measure they
drafted stipulated a minimum cash
margin of go per cent, abolished
numerous practices considered ques-
tionable, provided for corporate f1nan-
cial statements at frequent intervals
and gave the Tvade Commission re-
sponsibility for administration and
enforcement.


Wall Street quickly protested, find
ing objections in nearly every section
of the measure, but protesting princi-
pally the phases of the bill outlined
above. The group of experts divided
into two factions in disagreement over
modifying the margin requirements.


Then the administration stepped in,
President Roosevelt directing the
Treasury and Federal Reserve Board
to investigate the effect of the meas
ure on Government finances and the
banks.

gala opening of Seaside Park this

that visitors will hardly recognize
the place.

the park is nearing completion.

was swept away in a storm last
fall is now located in a section Of
the casino, thus becoming much
more accessible to resort visitors.

dancers in the Seaside ballroom
this season. Frank Flanagan, long
a member of Frank Slaughter's
Orchestra, will direct a seven-piece
unit.


Frequent train service from the
District line will be provided daily
starting Saturday. Roads are re-
ported in fine condition all the
way to Seaside.

Heroic attempts to rescue the help
less members of the Usworth's crew
were described by Capt. Sadie Con-
thier, master of the rescue ship Jean
Jadot, in a wireless dispatch to the
Associated Press.


As the seas rolled furiOusly in a
wild storm of hurricane force the Jean
Jadot launched q lifeboat carrying 10
members of her crew who volunteered
for the rescue attempt. The Ascania
stood by, pouring hundreds Of tons OF
oil on the oceans surface.


The Jean Jadot's boat finally came
alongside the Usworth, Capt. Gonthier
said, and started taking off her crew.


1t was perilous job, for the sea
kept hurting the rescue boat against
the Usworth's sides and the freighter' s
men were forced to slide down line
to reach the Jean Jadot,s boat.


Eight men had been taken off the
freighter when huge wave swamped
the little boat and it became folled
in cargo derricks hanging over the
side of the Usworth. The rescue boat
edged away, rolling in the raging sea.
Suddenly another big wave swept over
the frail boat and it capsized, with its
18 passengers plunging helplessly into
the water.


The Jean Jabot rushed another boat
over the side and managed to pick
up 8 of the 10 volunteers and two of
the Usworth's crew.


The two men lost from the Jean
Jadot we're the fourth officer and an
other member of the crew.


Another Boat Launched.
The Ascania then launched boat
and took off other survivors while the
storm continued unabated.


The. Usworth was stricken helpless
about $50 miles east of Newfoundland
when giant waves smashed her steer
ing gear She sent out calls for help
and the Jean Jadot hurried to her as
sistance. The Belgian liner managed
to get lines aboard the Usworth and
was endeavoring to tow the helpless
boat to safety when the storm tore
the two vessels apart, and for 10 hours
they were separated.


Then came on S OS appeal from
the Usworth that her situation was
precarious and that the crew must be
taken of. The Jean Jadot and the
Ascania arrived to start their rescue
work with its tragic results. Details
regarding the deaths of the other sever
victims were not contained in the dis
patch from the Ascania.

VIENNA. November 27.-Austrian
students today attacked the Czecho-
slovak Legation in reprisal for recent
anti German riots at the university in
Praha, capital Of Czechoslovakia. but
were repulsed by police who battered
them with swords and clubs.


Vienna was thrown into fresh tur-
moil by the demonstrations.


The students rained bricks and
stones at the Czech controlled news
papers. Der Tag and Die Tunde,
smashing almost every window in the
plants, wrecking the interior of the
offices and terrorizing the editors and
printers.


Then, several hundred strong, the
students marched to the Czech Lega-
tion shouting: Down with Czechoslo-
vakia; revenge our fellow students in
Praha."


Protected by Police.


They found the Czech Legation en-
circled by police who charged into
them with their sidearms failing.


Beaten of, they marched to the
StefansplatZ where the demonstration
assumed Nazi aspect. the students
singing the German national anthem,
Deutschland Uber Allies"


Mounted police charged into the
crowd which had gathered in the
Ringstrasse near the Czech Legation.
Several women and children waiting
for street cars were knocked down.

BY the Associated Press.


NEW ORLEANS, September ga
truce between Senator Huey Long
and Maor T. Semmes Walmsley
brought comparative peace to the
New Orleans battle-ground today.


The rivals for political control Of
the city agreed not to use armed men
at the polls in Tuesdays Democratic
primary-the howdown-unleSs they
were ordered out by an Arbitration
Committee.


Mayor Walmsley also accepted one
point in the dictatorial program in
stituted by Senator Long. He gave
recognition to the parole powers
granted to the police jury commits
sioners by the State Legislature
which conferred upon Long his
powers. -


Damper Put on Warfare.


This composure of differences put
a damper on the strong talk that had
thundered forth between the op-
posing camps, and the pOpllace of
New Orleans itself was calm.


Long. nevertheless, held his 1000
State Militiamen encamped in the
Jackson Barracks and under the
wharf sheds of the Dock Board along
the river front, fringing the business
section Of the city. Walmsley's po-
lice, $500 strong, maintained their
positions within the city.


Beyond the city limits anxious
citizens and parents of the youthful
National Guardsmen, fearing blood

pat, raise your index finger"

Breaking away from two members
of the construction crew replacing the
old Benning Bridge, an unidentified
young woman leaped into the Ana
costa River this morning, floundered
on the surface for several minutes as
she tried to reach the shore and sank
after the current swept her 100 yards
north of the bridge. Harbor precinct
policemen recovered the body shortly
before noon.


The construction foreman had
caught the woman shortly before she
leaped. He saw her come running onto
the east end of the bridge, sobbing
wildly. The woman climbed over the
concrete railing and was clinging to
the outer side Of the bridge, with her
feet on small ledge when the fore
man graSped her.


Leave me alone!" the woman cried.
Leave me alone!"


The foreman held on and shouted
for help. A workman came running,
and together the two men hauled her
back over the rail and set her on the
sidewalk.


OuMUS hdliuB again.
Immediately, the woman started
running toward the center of the
bridge. The workmen told police
they supposed she had changed her
mind about committing suicide and
would go away.


Once out of reach of the men, the
woman again climbed the railing and
this time did not hesitate before leap
ing.


She hit the water fiat, and appar-
emily was partially stunned. She
could swim a little, however, and
after moment began to strive des-
perately to reach shore, only about
10 yards away.


But the current. converted at this
point into a swift channel by the
construction work, slowly forced her
peared and sank again finally in the
muddy water near the opposite bank.


Boat Rescue Fails.
While the woman struggled, several
workmen ran off the bridge and
launched a boat from the bank be-
meath. They were too late to reach
her side.


She was a small brunette about
% years old. The woman was bare
headed and wore light cotton house
dress.


Police also were unable to learn
whether the woman came to the
bridge on foot or in an automobile.
No one seems to have seen her before
she ran onto the bridge


Once in the river the woman
struggled in silence and made no
response to shouted advice from the
bridge.


Police removed the body to the
District Morgue, where it remained
unidentified at late hour today.

The revised stock market control

BY the Associated Press.


DENTON. Tex. November 30.-The
death in flames of Miss Helen Gard
ner, 18-year-old student at the North
Texas State Teachers College, puzzled
authorities today.


Screaming in agony, the attractive
coed was found in the bathtub at her
roming house, her nude body covered
with blazing towels. The towels ap-
parently had been soaked in a highly
inflammable fluid and then ignited.
The door of the bath room was locked.


Hearing the screams, several other
roomers and Mrs. M c. Henry, at
whose home the girl lived, battered
down the locked door and smothered
the flames. Miss Gardner lost con-
sciousness soon after being rushed to
a hospital and died last night.

BERLIN, July Fear rode the
streets of Berlin today and deepened
the hue of blue Monday as reports
of further disturbances were whis-
pered about.


Everyone fears the secret police.


Crowds filed past the Wilhelm
strasse Building in which Chancellor
Hitler, with Ministers Goering and
Goebbels were giving orders for literal
determination of all those suspected
of connection with anti-Nazi party
plotting.


Police Ready to Act.


Police marched by twos, with rifles
on their shoulders, ready for instant
action If 1t were needed.


The mystery Of what was going on
inside the buildings on the Wilhelm
strasse remained as deep as ever for
the man in the street. Little informa-
ton could be had beyond quietly ped
died rumors.


1t was apparent to all that Hitler
and Goering were, in the present sit
uation at least, firmly in the saddle.


With principal leaders of the op-
position already dead and other
shootings rumored hourly, opposing
forces had no directing heads to lead
them into action.


Government buildings were still
heavily guarded. The black-shirted
Schultz Staffel, Goering's special
guardsmen, were held in readiness for
any emergency.


Berlin was going about its business.
but the atmosphere was still tensely
charged as rumors foated back and
forth through the streets.


In these rumors France emerged as
the mysterious foreign power" which
Hitler charged Saturday with having
been In communication with the con-

SANTA BARBARA, Calf, July a.
On the verge of death three days
ago, Marie Dressler clung stubbornly
to life today despite the seemingly
fatal complications Of cancer and
uremic poisoning.


Last Thursday night the 62-year-
old actress sank so low that attend
ing physicians expressed the belief
she could not live until morning, but
an amazing vitality since then has
restored consciousness to her and she
has been able to take liberal amount
of liquid nourishment.


Occasionally she speaks to attend
ants, doctors said, and she has been
able to obtain a considerable amount
of needed rest.


She slept with comfort on Friday
and Saturday nights and dozed most
Of Sunday. Her pulse has kept q
steady, almost normal beat since
Thursday night, when her heart ac-
tion suddenly became normal after
life had all but died out, and her
temperature has ranged about two
degrees above normal.

LONDON (P.-A recent survey
shows British voters aren't interested
in international questions.


They want to know only about ma
tional problems that affect them indi-
vidually, such as unemployment relief,
aid for shipping and industry and
agriculture, and what hours they will
find the bars open.


Conservative leaders found out all

is thinking by a careful canvass Of
the country.

dismayed some leaders who had be-
lieved the party's India policy would
top the list of questions asked.


Caravans Sound Opinions.

recently from London in various di-
rections. Each caravan had its
speaker and government propaganda
movie films


In each place where a SHOW" was
held, the speakers asked the assem-
bled voters to state their views on
national and world problems.


The expressions of opinions, to-
gether with the usual questions fired
by the citizens at the speakers, gave
the Tories lot to think about.


In most areas, not even Sir Oswald
Mosley and his Fascists were referred
to-. Few people seemed interested in
India. None cared what happened to
foreign nations.


Equipped With Duds.


All the people asked about were
local and home questions of the
moment.


Most of the speakers were well pre-
pared to discuss the future of India,
international politics and similar
problems, but they had little use for
such information.


India may be a big matter for
politicians and for Parliament, and
may be the major subject before
Parliament next session, but the
voters seem aloof and uninterested, +"

BY the Associated Press.


PEGS, Hungary, October 16.-
Twelve hundred suicide striking
miners came out Of their pits alive
today on promises of better pay, but
expressed dissatisfaction with the
offer which had kept them from dying
under ground.


One miner, speaking for his COM
rades, said: THE new terms. offered
by the company are no good. We
accepted them because we were de-
mented."


What the miners underwent below
ground probably will mean suicide
for some of them, for q few are In
such a critical condition from their
priyations and underground air
poisoning that physicians said they
feared they might die.


Ito Crowding Hospitals. :.


Hospitals were crowded with iio
Of the 'sresurrected" miners who,
when they were brought out Of their
black pit, looked like starved beggars,
with their faces covered with whis-
kers and their clothes in tatters.


The miners dissatisfaction with the
company's settlement was also shared
by the townspeople. Shopkeepers sold
the miners and their families bread
and bologna on credit and fund was
started to give them charity.


Not too soon did the men bring to
q close their self-imposed imprison-
ment. The semi-conscious men were
suffering from gas poisoning and ex-
-posure after ITO hours In the pits.


Even the more robust were haggard,
but joyful.


The men will receive Winter bonus
Of So each, and instead of an 8 per
cent wage cut, a Christmas bonus of
the same amount.


Welcomed by Families.


There were dramatic scenes as the
miners reached the pit mouth, to be
welcomed by wives and children, who
had waited long days for the moment
Soldiers and militiamen with ma
chine guns and rifles, also waited, and
gave the mine surface the appearance
of an army camp. There appeared to
be no cause for trouble, however. Men
and women alike were joyful at the
outcome.


Police denied any men perished in
the pits.


ITO Hours In Earth.


For 110 hours the men had re-
manned deep in the earth, sending
back word they preferred death to
surrender. They wanted more money
and more work than the 50 and two
days weekly they have been getting.


With fanatical zeal they rejected
pleas sent down by q frantic govern
tic wives. But this morning q com.
promise was accepted.


Mine owners and the government
reached an agreement. Peace ennis
saries were allowed by the strikers
guards to 60 below with the offer and
the men debated. At daylight they
came out.


Troops Watch.


Government troops stood behind ma
chine guns as the men emerged, but
there was no disorder. Today this
mining town celebrated, for the most
heart-rending experience in its history
was over.


Only q few hours before the settle
ment, the desperate miners threatened
to kill Gen. Janos Estergalyos, member
Of Parliament, who tried to mediate
with them.

turn after very dull first hour, and

hundred onion weeders reiterated
through their leader, Okey Odell, their
intentions to "see the thing through. +"


Herbert Radcliffe, leader of a corps
of deputy sheriffs, said one deputy was
cut on the hand and several strikers
were injured by clubs when 10 of
those arrested offered resistance.


Radcliffe said deputies fired several
shots from a machine gun at five men
they found in woods. The deputies
sought to search the five men for
weapons after reports that shots had
been fired in the district. The quintet,
however, fed into the cornfleld.


Radcliffe said the strikers had at
tempted to stop five carloads and one
truckload of outside workers being
escorted into the Scioto marshland
onion fields by Earl Huston, major
grower.


Radcliffe said knives, sling-shots
and rocks were taken from the
strikers.

text:
Special Dispatch to The Star.


NEW YORK, December 29.-With
the volume of trade during the Christ
mastide breaking records for the last
five years, many merchants in this
city have set sail for a weeks vaca-
ton, leaving year-end inventory tax
ing to their junior partners.


Equally tired physically, but eager
for holiday week in New York, were
the numerous out-of-town buyers who
arrived here the last few days. They
turned detailed stock-taking over to
assistants as they sought merchan-
disc to repleniSh much depleted in
ventories.


Manufacturers, many of whom re-
ported plant activities at the highest
rate at this season in five years, were
too busy to pay much attention to
forecasting or inventories, as they
sought to supply fresh merchandise
or complete Spring lines.


Retail trade this week in many sec
tionS was only moderate, for unlike
the last three or four years holiday
clearance merchandise was not on
hand and hence could not be pro-
NOTED. Wholesale markets were busy
with the usual January merchandise


Booked for Celebrations.


Railroads, steamships. hotels, res
taurants and clubs are heavily booked
for year-end celebrations. Liquor
orders are far ahead Of a year ago.
Cigar jobbers here report the best
Christmas trade since 1929 in domes-
tic products and the best they can
remember for most types of Havana
cigars which, because of the lowered
duty growing out of the reciprocal
trade agreement, have been reduced in
price.


Completion of additional reciprocal
trade pactS has cheered importers and
exporters. With our foreign trade for
the first l months well above the COR
responding period of 1888, and the
trade of Canada and Japan, likewise
showing improvement. shipping COM
panies expect world trade to flow more
freely next year.


Buyers for Brazilian and Colombian
houses were here this week to arrange
Tor purchases as soon as trade agree
ments are signed by their govern
ments. Most of the visitors were
chiefly interested in agricultural i'm
plements, machine tools, business ma
chimes and Office equipment. Export
ers believe many Latin American buy
ers will visit leading American mar
kets over the next six weeks.


Most of the leading industries in
the final week Of 1884 were either
operating at higher rate than a year
ago or were showing good net gains
for the year compared with 1888.
Wool. tin. cotton, silk, sugar MEETINGS
and lumber output were exceptions to
this general trend.


Steel Operations Climb.


Steel operations, for the tenth sue
ceSSlve week, were stepped up. with
capacity for this period the highest
since 1929. Building is much ahead
of year ago, and that is true of gen.
eral construction, despite the storms
in the last few days. Mills are turning
out more wheat flour, factories more
boots and shoes and refineries are
handling more crude petroleum for the
week as well as for the year. Electric
power was ahead of any week in the
last four years and not much below
its record week in 1929.


Bituminous coal has been stepped I'D
to meet increasing domestic and in
dustrial demand. Tobacco is far ahead
OF a year ago. Anthracite, kerosene,
lubricating oil. zinc, tires, lead. meat
packing, pig iron, cement. heavy and
fine chemicals and automobiles. both
passenger and truck. also are at higher
production rates than a year ago.


Commodity prices generally are we'll
above year ago, with predictions that
many of them will advance or hold
firm for the next few months. Ex-
ceptions to the upward trend are lead,
wool, raw sugar, gasoline, silk, refined
sugar, pine flooring, tin and burlap.


Retail food prices average the high
est levels since December 4. 1880, ac-
cording to Dun & Bradstreet, Inc,
who point out that rise of S cents
during the week, due chiefly to grains
and meats and their products, was
one of the sharpest this year.

after the officer had taken the

holding the officer at bay under

banbits drove into Hooking

Fishing over the weekend has
been completely washed out by the
rains of the past few days.


1t is a shame, too, because re-
ports from various sources leaned
decidedly toward the prospects of
a great period OF successful assault
and battery on the blues and trout,
particularly the latter.


Trout Fishing


Ralph Murdock and Palmer
Sewers did some splendid trout
fishing Sunday over the Chinese
Mud bottom which lies between
the steamboat channel and Solo
mons Island, fishing with Captain
Rody Langley.


Just after dawn and in an
hours time they yanked in IS of
the black beauties averaging just
under two pounds. They stopped
biting as suddenly as they had
started.


Later in the day these two, with
Mrs. Murdock, went out again.
They fiShed at one spot for 30
minutes without a nibble. They
moved to another and almost i'm
mediately Mrs. Murdock hooked
412pound trout, which was boated
with difficulty. Forty-two more
trout fell prey, including another
4-pounder.


Larry Homan and Ed Jameson
also had a fine trip off the Sand
Gates in the Patuxent, pulling in
10 plump trout and Is sizable
hardheads with fresh shrimp.
They found the fishing best just
before and just after dark.


Soft she'll crabs are disappear
ing rapidly from around the lower
Potomac and consequently are too
expensive for bait. Fishermen
around Breton Bay. Kopel's Point
and Blackstone Island are using
shrimp and bloodworms effectively
in catching trout, blues, hard
heads and spots.

CARPINTERIA, Calf, June 18.-
Frontier stage coach drivers will
gather Saturday to recall the days
when the long, rawhide whip ex-
ploded over the heads of plunging
horses as America moved westward.


Four pioneer residents have ar
ranged a reunion of the fast dimln-
ishing legion. Col. Fred Richardson,
John E. Jones, Selin Carrillo and
Mai. Joel Rimington Fithian, each
veteran who topped a concord in the
days when highwaymen and Indians
made travelling hazardous, are seek.
ing members of that once colorful
and thriving work.


Our only desire is to form a per-
manent organization of the remaining
members of one of the most danger
Gus and colorful crafts in the history
of the West before all of them are
gone. with their most thrilling stories
unrecorded, and their exciting careers
unsung," Richardson said.


Dick Fellows, Joaquin Murieta and
other notorious outlaws terroriZed
the highways in the Cos and 70s to
make the stage coach runs difficult.
Heavily armed guards perched atop
the rough-riding coaches. Gun
fights with the robbers were frequent.

A NNAPOLIS, Md, September 20.
~ Navy fired a broadside for
~ all Army to see today, easily


winning its opening gridiron
duel against William and Mary, 20 to
Z. Fred Berries personally accounted
for all the sailors touchdowns.


With capacity crowd of $4,000, in
cluding the regiment just returned
from leave or hand to witness the
debut of Coach Thomas ]. Hamilton's
first production, the Navy varsity
made quick work of scoring twice in
first period. 1t then retired and al
lowed the reserves to battle the Vir-
ginians most of the way.


Rushed back into the fray late in
the third period, the varsity tailed on
its second play as Berries, 177-pound
shifty back from Louisville, KY, broke
through for 47-yard goalward dash.


Surprise Pass Works.
THE Indians, first game opponent


for the Middies for the last six


years, threw their only scare into
Navy in the last period on a surprise
pass from a substitute fullback. Regi-
nald Pinch, to Halfback Stumpy
Bryant that the William and Mary
back carried Al yards over the goal
after a hip-swaying exhibition of
broken-field running.


Berries, the 22-year- old first class
man who does most of the ball carry
ing under the foot ball system brought
by Hamilton from California, sent the
future admirals to the front before
the game was three minutes old


After running an Indian punt back
20 yards to William and Mary's 25,
Berries struck out around left end, cut
back sharply and raced across the goal
as Beppo Lambert, Borries' pal and
roommate, personally blocked out
pair Of Indians and left the way clear
Five minutes later Berries scored
again, diving yards over center for
the touchdown after leading a mid
shipman offensive that began as he
hauled down an Indian kick on his
own 27.


Another for Berries.


TROM there on until the Navy
+ varsity returned in the third


period, the contest was a nip
and-tuck affair. With neither side
able to make any dangerous scoring
gestures. However, Navy pushed down
within the Indians 30 on three oc-
casions only to have holding penalties
shove them back and interrupt their
rallies.


Borries' last touchdown was his most
thrilling contribution. Apparently
entangled in the midst Of Indian sec
ondary tacklers, the Kentucky boy
lodged and pivoted his way into the
clear and, with his knees almost
striking his chin as he pounded across
the chalk lines, raced 47 yards for the
final tally.


Woodward and Bryant. speedy Vir-
g1nians, broke loose time after time
in returning punts. but were seldom
able to slip past the sailors tacklers
after the play had settled down around
midfield.

THIS very interesting immigrant

the southern border of Georgia to

Rican mole cricket, also called the
ground puppy" is creeping about un-
der ground, making her tunnels as she
goes after food. Tobacco, peanuts,
grasses and truck crops are some OF her
favorite foods. The light soil in which
these plants are grown makes 1t easy
for her to ply her trade and make her
endless burrows.


Although this cricket belongs to the
same family as the famous cricket OF
the hearth and the field cricket, 1t is
only family resemblance. The name
mole comes from the velvety appear
ance Of the creature. This engineer Is
clothed in light brown, with under
parts still lighter and tinged with green.
The entire body Is covered with fine
hairs that makes it look like the famous
mole that goes about making tunnels.


The hind part of the crickets body is
soft, the chest and head are covered
with armor, used to push the dirt away
as the traveller goes about seeking food.
The front feet are shovel-shaped, stout
and short. They are very proficient
when it comes to digging away the dirt
from the seeds or plants that are be-
ing sought for their next meal.


The grown cricket has two pairs Of
wings, which are folded neatly along
the back. You can see the tips of the
hind wings. They reach beyond the tip
of the body, and look as If the lady was
in a hurry and forgot to tuck her
mighty" away. You have seen the
famous little ladybird beetle look that
way, too.

surface of the ground for about one or
two inches below the surface. The
ridges are like those of the true mole.
on a greatly reduced scale. The seed
lings are uprooted and soon dry out and
die. The soil all about the seeds be-
comes too disturbed for the seeds to
sprout. The potatoes are nibbled. and

BERLIN, December 8.-Gen. Her
mann Goering and DR.. Joseph Goeb-
bels, seeking clothing for the poor,
nearly lost their own today.


The NaZi big-wigs were passing the
hat for the Winter relief fund, and
to prove incidentally that they do not,
as cabinet ministers, feel themselves
above appealing personally.


With collection boxes the burly-
cheSted, be-medalled Goering and the
slight, academic Goebbels took up a
stand outside the Unter Den Linden
Hotel. They became the center Of a
crowd of $4,000, which surged forward,
trampling children and elderly per-
sons to contribute their pfennigs.


Police were helpless in holding them
back. Goering stood his ground for
a while, then fled into the hotel and
out the back door.


Goebbels, whose propaganda genius
staged the day of national solidar-
ity" as part of the Winter campaign
in preparation for the forthcoming
hard months, Jared better. He filled
several contribution boxes, then took
off his hat and filled it. before being
obliged, like Goering, to seek shelter.


The day was great success.

THE shortage of wild ducks this year has
proven advantageous to another branch Of
sport-hunting for upland birds with dogs.


From Saskatchewan comes word that trainers
of hunting dogs find that this year the dogs
are keeping their noses, hguratively speaking, in
their own business. The prairie ponds of the
province in the past have geen great nuisance
to the trainers because they have usually been
well populated with wild ducks and wild duck
on a pond often proved more interesting to the
dogs than a bird to be hunted in the upland
sections.

flock of ducks throughout the Summer, when
normally the ponds would have been teeming
with the birds.

as Thief Lake report that the nesting grounds
are only about 40 per cent populated, which
indicates the serious effect of the drought and
the overshooting of the past season

HOTEVILLA, Third Mesa, Ariz.
August 25.-The faith of the Hopi
people is undergoing a severe test.


For the first time in years rain has
failed to follow the annual snake
dance.


Reptile messengers to the under
world gods of moisture were released
as the sun sank redly last night
Purified in elaborate rituals and
Sprinkled with sacred meal, the snakes
Slithered away into the desert, carry
ing the Hopi prayers and pledges OF
fealty to the irate gods who hold in
their hands the rain-giving thunder
bolts.


Then the Hopi waited-in vain.


The red eye of the sun still glowered
today from the hot arch of simmer
ing sky. Thunder rolled briefly across
the far horizon, but the rain drops il
loosed passed the Hopis mesas by.


The water gods of the underworld
were not yet appeased.


Tomorrow the Hopi desperately will
try again.

NEW YORK. August 22.-New life

MACON, Ga, May 25.-A strange
friendship between a 3-year-old boy
and 2-foot snake was disclosed by
the boys parents, who do not know
just what to do about it.


Mrs. James F. Posey recently no
ticed her son Edward taking scraps of
bread from the table and hiding them
in closet. Since the boy had no
pets, she inquired about the case, but
the reply she got was that the bread
was for Buddy.


She later saw Edward sitting on the
floor holding Buddy, the snake, and
feeding it break crumbs The horri-
fled mother ran from the room for
fear her presence would cause the
snake to bite the child


The parents said they were not try
ing to break up the pairs friendship
and expressed the belief the child and
snake had developed a fondness for
one another that exists between other
children and their dog or cat pets.


They have asked callers not to at
tempt to see the child and snake to-
gether for fear of frightening the
reptile, but Mrs. Posey opened the
closet door for a reporter.


Buddy was not at home, but bread
crumbs scattered about two holes in
the floor showed Edward had set the
table for his pal.

quarters about $3.50 pm. One Of the
men was armed with a razor, the
other with a gun, Brensfield said.

arms were tied, while the two men
planned to wait until / o'clock this
morning before plundering the resi-
dence.


The men worked in stocking feet,
leaving their shoes behind, and about
1880 Brensfeld worked himself loose
and called police from the sixth,
eighth and tenth precincts, who sur
rounded the place. Patrolman S. J.
Prophet captured Thomas in the
kitchen.


After the robbery Comdr. Graves
reported $40 was taken from his wal
let, while several hundred dollars
worth of jewelry and silverware was
overlooked.

No. 2.

its banks at some points and rapidly
rising this morning; several houses
in Falmouth and other low points
have been damaged.

opened Tuesday, has been practically
forced to suspend because of the heavy

INDIANAPOLIS, September 15.-
The home of Gilbert Jacobs and his
housekeeper. Mrs. Dimmie Dillon, was
searched today by officers investigate
ing the murder Of the woman's 13-
year-old son, Donald Edward Dillon.


DR.. John E. Wyttenbach, deputy
coroner, after poking through dingy
SUBJ basement, said the walls were
marked with six holes, apparently
made by bullets from small rifle.
He said he also found remnants of
clothing which bore stains that would
be analyzed to determine whether
they were made by human blood.


Jacobs, 37-year-old factory worker,
and Mrs. Dillon, S5-year-old divorce,
are held on vagrancy charges while
officers continue their investigation.


Donald's body came floating from
sewer last Tuesday following heavy
rainstorm. In the head were two
wounds made by bullets Of small
caliber and the body bore marks
which officers said indicated that the
boy was the victim of a person afflicted
with sadism. Mrs. Dillon had re-
ported to police Monday that her son
had been missing since Sunday night.


Mrs. Dillon was taken into custody
yesterday following her sons funeral.
Jacobs was arrested several hours
after the boys body was found.

ments which brought most of Para

raid from the north in an effort to
outflank the stoutly entrenched

pared was impregnable, appeared

Paraguays first and third corps, COM
manded by Coils. Delgado and
rernanoez, anu Gney were expected to

men in the field

P.-Two Coast Guard patrol boats
battling heaving seas, floating ice and
gales, today reached the leaking. rud-
derless fishing schooner Hope Leslie
took her in tow, and started with her
for Woods Hole.


The Patrol Boat 235, for whose
safety fears were felt after being un-
reported for hours, reached the help
less, drifting 80-foot schooner about
midforenoon and was joined later by
the CG lat.

race against time for the Coast
Guard base The schooner was TAX
ing on water fast and her crew of 10
labored at the pumps. trying to keep
the craft af1oat during the 15-mile
run to port.


The wind, which had been strong
southwest and warm, with rain all
night, had shifted to a freezing
northeast gale with snow squalls. The
change in the wind churned the ice
foes, making navigation extremely
dangerous.

beach apparatus on the sands, pre-
pared to take the 10 men off with a
breeches buoy. The schooner had
lain helpless 500 feet from shore
while her crew clung to the rigging
to keep from being washed over
board.

tors Slowed over temporarily con-
structed bridges made OF telephone
poles. hatch covers and lumber, cross
ing ceep crevices in the ice


About half the bulk of the expedi-
tions stores was maSsed in islands

In the center of the pressure area.
composed Of almost impossible ridges

tended as directional antennae for

Timbers that had been used to

age from Boston were employed as
and hatch covers from

Inevitably the bridge was named

to it were filled with snow and ice,
then the road across the bay was
shoveled out and ice distractions
Ieveled off with saws and crowbars


1t was a winding and tempestuous
road, and dog driver gave it the
name THE Bad Lands"


The weather continues astonishingly

dropping steadily. The last three
nights shifts have had to work in
of 10 to Is degrees be-

was clear, is now constantly overcast

NEW YORK, April 21.-Security

the dollar.


Stock trading was the most active
for a Saturday in several weeks, total

weakness appeared to have been less
of market factor. Perhaps it was
offset by the uncertainty during buSi-
ness hours as to what success the sill
yer bloc would have with its demands

prices, both spot and futures, reacted
and some of the white metal shares
eaSed

explained by rumors circulating in
Europe to the effect that further dol
lar devaluation loomed. but there
were no surface developments to sup
port such gossip. French francs. it
was pointed out, were probably re-
flecting the stronger gold position of

newly balanced budget.

During construction the huge pier
resembled from above an immense
honey comb, except the wells" were
round. These wells of heavy steel
we're capped with domes and were
kept af1oat by compressed air while
concrete was poured into the inter

had been cleaned by high pressure
streams of water.

bedrock to a few feet above the high
water mark and will be built up 280
feet more.

is the distinctive feature of the cros-

their flat, virtually under lock and
key. Why the father had kept
him a prisoner remained unclear
to investigators.


In 1915, court records show, the
father filed a complaint that his
wife kept the boy locked up at the
age of years.


Young Kratzner, thin and sal.
low, answered questions jerkily
and in a high voice.

Dillinger'S escape was the Sec

Obtaining the machine guns,

Gun" Carved From Wood

Dillinger was able to proceed

Don't move or I'll fill you

Had Merry Time


The teams recent home stand
has made the situation a new
and thoughtful one. Always
powerful on their own lot, the
Yanks have had a merry time
while entertaining the West.
Every series was won with the
exception of a four-game set with
the Detroit Tigers, which found
the clubs each two contests.


Naturally, the team climbed-so
much, in fact, that the present
first-place position was secured.
The skeptics are wondering what
helped the Mccarthy men, aside
from their usual success while
playing at home.


Pitching is the answer. This was
never better demonstrated than

set the Griffs down with three

Gomez Effective


Then too, Lefty Gomez has

Johnny Murphy and Johnny
Broaca, recruit right-handers, who

sons as big league hurlers.


To look at the remainder OF the
team, one could almost say it was
not of championship caliber due
to several flaws here and there
But it's been winning games just
the same, and after all, that's
what counts.


Manager Mccarthy has been
forced to make many change in
the lineup since the opening of
the campaign, but because the
pitching has braced in recent
weeks, these changes have not
been handicap.


For example, two important in
juries befell the team recently
when Tony Lazzeri and Earl
Combs were injured. Mccarthy
put the uncertain Don Heffner at
second in Lazzeri's place, while he
moved Ben Chapman to center as
Combs substitute, and inserted
Myrl Hoag in left field.

Then in the infield he's had
to make several big changes
Red Rolfe began at short, but
illness forced him on the side
lines. Jack Saltzgaver was re
called from Newark to play thirc

With all these supposed handl
caps the Yanks have continued
to win-even with the fading
Babe Ruth in right field as ar
additional worry-and the team
promises to continue on winning
providing the great pitching
holds the pace it has set for Itself
in recent weeks.

Richmond, Va.-FOur Of the
five cOnvicts who escaped early
today from the Virginia State
Penitentiary were captured
shortly after noon in the woods
just beyond the State Prison
Farm in GOOchland county, rs
miles north of here. Wexford
Hayden, cOlored, serving life for
murder, is the only one still at
large.


Five desperate criminals, known
to be armed, were being sought in
the District this afternoon follow
ing a spectacular jailbreak from
the Virginia State Penitentiary in
Richmond in which they kidnapped
a matron and used her for
shield to prevent guards from fir
ing on them.


Three of the men are murder
ers, while the other two are bank
robbers, who used a machine gun
in robbing a Lee county bank sew
eral months ago.


First Auto Found


The men stole an automobile
near the prison and headed for
Washington. This car was later
found abandoned on the highway
80 miles north, and authorities be-
lieve they stole a second machine
to throw off pursuit.


The men overpoWered q guard
while cleaning up in the women's
ward of the prison, took his keys
and gun, then forced the matron
to accompany them until they
were safe in the machine.


Guards were unable to fire on
the men for fear hitting the
woman.


The men who escaped were Will
liam Lynn and Edward Veal, each
serving As years for bank robbery,
and three colored murderers, Clai-
borne Layne and Wexford Hayden,
serving life. and Paul Austin, serv-
ing 81 years.


All Roads Guarded


The spectacular jailbreak was
made at $50 this morning, when
the five men, directed by Guard
J. w. Coffey, went to the Women's
quarters to clean up.


Two of the men suddenly
turned on the guard and seized
him, while another secured his
pistol and keys. They then seized
the matron, Mrs. Virginia Spen-
GER, unlocked the door and STEP
ped out into the street, using her
for shield.


AS they sped away an alarm
was sounded, and all roads were
guarded by State and county pc.
lice.


Shortly after the break the
car with the escaped convicts
sped by the State prison farm.
Guards there opened fire on
the machine.


May Have Helpers


A short distance from the farm
the car was found abandoned,
and posse was organized and
started to beat the woods nearby,
but found no trace of the men.


1t is believed that the men
stole another car or that accom-
plices provided another machine.


Washington police were notified
of the break and placed guards
at all bridges.

CARLISLE, Pa, December 1.-The
Blue Ridge Mountains tonight enfold
the bodies of the three little girls
in Pennsylvania mysterious babes
in the wood" tragedy.


Residents Of the historic Cumber-
land Valley bore them there through
the rain today with the same tender
ness they would have shown were
they their own.


Several hundred men, women and
children stood bareheaded in the
downpour while the white caskets were
lowered into muddy graves on the
fringe of the broad, fiat, pine-studded
cemetery. which holds the remains Of
some of the valleys most distinguished
people.


Few Go to Cemetery.


The services we're brief and only
a few cars followed the three hearses
to the mountain cemetery after two
Protestant ministers and a Catholic
priest prayed for the dead at the
l25-year-old mansion that is now a
funeral parlor.

the Legion quartet sang a hymn.
Hundreds stood in the street hoping
for a glimpse into the softly lighted
room.


Then. Boy Scouts. Girl Scouts and
Girl Reserves bore the floral pieces
to waiting cars. State police, guard
ing the doors, made path through
the onlookers, and the caskets were
removed to the hearses.

of its members dabbed their eyes with
handkerchiefs.

to investigation of the mystery case

the children with the man and wom-

10. and Norma, II.

has identified Noakes through finger
prints, and the children's grand

tossed over in the running seas. Prev
iously, the Jean Jadot's lifeboat had
carried five of the Usworth's crew to
safety and presumably had gone back
to get another load of the 81 members
of the crew still aboard the sinking
ship.

before dawn and was answered by the
Jean Jadot and the Cunarder Ascania,
the latter standing by to lower her
own boats shortly after the Jean

TINE polo season was away wing


ing here yesterday afternoon


as the seasoned War Depart
i men team tapped out smart


victory over the reckless young
men Of Pennsylvania Military Col
lege. Whatever praise or blame the
riders earned on the turf of Potomac
Park certainly was not accorded in
seclusion. Every inch of parking
space around the field was packed.
Hundreds, literally thousands, sat in
cars and watched. Scores came on
foot and perched on the long green
benches, beneath spreading shade
trees, while the lean ponies raced back
and forth. their bandaged tails flag
ging vigorously as they ran.


Polo shares the fascination of all
caselessly moving sports - hockey,
tennis, base ball. The intervals be-
tween play are brief; almost always
there is some swift, spectacular action
afoot. Therefore 1t draws such crowds
as will be seen at no other equestrian
events. There are fewer experts and
addicts on hand, more novitiates and
those who came purely for thrill.

Special Dispatch to The Star.


NEW YORK, October 23.-"What
will the President say to bankers
tomorrow" That's the greeting in
Wall Street today. instead Of the
usual whats new?"


Wall Street barely hurdles. crawls
under, or goes around one obstacle
when 1t sees another. Now that
third-quarter earnings are showing up
better than had been expected q
few weeks ago, the Street has manu-
factured another obstacle-President
Roosevelts address to the American
Bankers Association at the convention
in Washington next Wednesday.


This constant handicapping of mar
kets through more or less manufac-
tured worry about future events prob
ably hurts the Street and its clientele
more than regulation or threatened
legislation.


The return to Washington of secur-
tiles exchange commission aides who
have been comforting here with special
lists directs attention to the fact trat
the Securities Exchange Commission
has not yet established any New York
Office. Eventually the Securities Ex-
change Commission will have Offices in
several cities throughout the country.
Its completed staff may reach 300, in
stead of the 800 originally contem-
plated. The taxpayer, however. need
not worry about the extent of Securl-
ties Exchange Commission activities,
since he is not paying for them.
Gamblers, spectators and investors
pay all the expense of the Securities
Exchange Commission.


David Saperstein, Leon Cohen and
James A. Fayne did most Of the talk
ing. here with specialists, and some
rules regarding specialists activities
may be announced any day. Thus
far, the question of regulating short
selling has not been considered. This
will be taken up when specialists
rules are finished.


Despite their lack Of office space,
the Securities Exchange Commission
men are making real progress
on a great number Of problems all
over the country.


The merger of the two Los Angeles
exchanges is expected to enlarge the
Pacific Coast market In New York
Stock Exchange issues. Presumably
prices in Los Angeles will follow rather
than lead quotations on the New York
Stock Exchange. Both sets of quota
tions, however. will have to be followed
closely, because both must be con-
Sidered in fixing the lowest price for
margin calculations.


Members of the New York Stock
Exchange. despite time difference, will
not be able to arbitrage between here
and Los Angeles, since exchange
rules prohibit arbitraging in q domes-
tic market in securities listed here.
Nevertheless, the exchange merger,
and the widening of markets on the
coast for local Stock Exchange issues,
are raising many questions that are
keeping the Securities EXCHANGE Com
mission busy.

flame we'll above the derrick that had
been built to make the proceedings
more realistic.

between the flame and the source of
the fuel for a split second-long
enough to separate the two per-
manently.

GENEVA, December 27.-Oil-

peared likely last night to increase the

Zeal for acquisition of valuable oil
fields was seen here as one of the fac
tors likely to complicate the dispute as
Rome and Adds Ababa added two
more notes to the League of Nations
growing file of documents relating to
the disagreement.


The two latest communications gave
directly contradictory versions Of the
events along the Ethiopian Italian
Somaliland border which have embit-
tered the relations between the two
countries.


Situation Serious.


A message from the Ethiopian gov
ernment termed the situation in
creasingly serious and charged Italian
troops with occupying Ethiopian towns


Romes statement bluntly denied the
accusations and in turn asserted that
Ethiopia had committed 'an act of
flagrant aggression"


Meanwhile, reports received here
told of the discovery of oil districts in
the controverted area, which the
Ethiopian press was said to be de-
scribing as partly responsible for the
dispute.


League circles expressed concern
that conflicting claims for the much
coveted natural resource might aggra-
vate the situation A similar clash is
regarded by some observers as the
cause for prolongation of the Chaco
war between Paraguay and Bolivia.


Constructing Highways.


Ethiopia's renewed protest to the
League today charged Italian troops
with constructing motor highways
simultaneously with their alleged in
vasion of Ethiopian territory. The
Italian advance, the complaint said,
was moving from Wardair toward Ado
and Gerlogubi in Ethiopia.


Although Ethiopia refrained from
appealing 10 UIS League ullutT d utll-

Italy, in It's message. emphatically

Paraguay May Accept Terms.

over the possibility that Paraguay
would accept the Leagues plan for
termination of the hostilities in the
Chaco boreal Paraguayan victories,

position, which the Bolivians assert
will give them possession Of the oil
regions.

formal protest from Persia against

Iraq mad appealed to the League,
saying the situation threatened to
disturb peace.

tend the session of the League Coun-

year, the entomologists reported.

BY the Associated Press.


PENSACOLA, Fla, January 5.-After
whipping up lofty waterspouts in the
harbor here yesterday, two tornadoes
lashed suddenly at the city, leaving one
dead, five persons injured and property
damage estimated at 100000.


Three-year-old Marion Kenneth Rigby
died today of injuries.


One of the storms lashed westward
along the waterfront, turned northward
along the edge of the business section
and veered again to the northeast,
striking Negro section and leaving a
swath $50 feet wide and 3 blocks long


At least 80 houses were demolished
in the Negro section. Debris was blown
half mile.


The other storm skirited the shore
and blew a roof off magazine at the
naval air station. The Rigby child was
blown from the arms of his father and
tossed against tree, 200 feet away.

Two cups milk, one cup canned
corn. one cup bread crumbs. one
tablespoon butter, one cup grated
cheese, two eggs, salt, pepper.

blended together. and stir until
slightly thickened. Season with

TOXIC, June 3O.-The japanese
NAVY feared a loss of at least l3 men
today in the crash of two warships and
what appeared to be another tragedy,
this one in the air.


Four men were known dead, two
were missing and four were injured
after the new 1.700-ton destroyers
Miyuki and Inazuma rammed together
last night during fleet maneuvers.


Three naval airplanes had been miss
ing for more than 80 hours with a
crew totaling nine.


The planes. attached to the aircraft
carrier Akagi. left NagasaN this
morning bound for Sasebo. The coast
was foggy. Other planes and warshlps
have been searching for them since
last night.


Both the Miyuki and Inazuma were
cruising at high speed when they col
lided. The formers stern was smashed
off. sinking Immediately. but the
larger portion Of the vessel remained
afoat. The Inazuma was almost a
total wreck. with her bows torn of.


Wreckage of the Inazuma and the
Miyuki were being towed today to the
naval base at Sasebo by the Cruiser
Naka and the destroyer Shirayuki.


Admiral Mineo Osumi. minister OF
navy, visited the palace and reported
the disaster to Emperor Hirohito.


The naval tragedy was Japans worst
since the torpedo boat Tomozuru
swamped and overturned in heavy seas
in March with 1l3 men aboard. Only
l3 of them were saved.


This disaster had national political
repercussions.

By the Associated Press.


ROSARIO. Argentina, September
S.-Three hundred and fifty des-
perate, shouting convicts mysteriously
equipped with rifles, pistols, hand
grenades and dynamite rioted madly
here yesterday in an unavailing break
for freedom.


A convict was killed and another
gravely wounded before flying squads
of military police and firemen man
aged to quell the disorders with tear
gas and fire hose.


The riot started early this morning
when inmates of the first cell block
marched into the patio for morning
exercises.


A revolver shot furnished the signal,
and Immediately bedlam broke loose
as the bowling rioters fired other
shots and set of hand grenades.


The din set prisoners in other cell
blocks to shouting but the guards
organized their defenses and confined
the would-be jail-breakers to the first
cell block and the patio.


An investigation was Immediately
launched to determine how the prison.
ers got their arms and the 60-pound
dynamite bomb with which they
planned to blast their way to free
dom.

By the Associated Press.


VIENNA, March 1.-The armed
strength Of strife-torn Austria has
been rapidly increasing since the
bloody Socialist civil war, and today
the government has at least 10000
armed men to deal with emergencies.


During the bitterest days Of the
recent fighting the government issued
numerous appeals to volunteers and
many responded.


The Fascist Heimwehr (home guard)
Is still conducting a vigorous campaign
for recruits.


Latest figures of Heimwehr Strngth
published in the newspaper of Vice
Chancellor Emil Fey-give $1,000
as the number of armed Fascists
throughout Austria. The regular
army has 10000 men and the police
gendarmerie exceeds $4,000, making
q total Of at least 10000 fighters.


Figures May Increase.


II Austro-German tension and the
internal dissension continue these
figures naturally are likely to be con-
siderably increased. In admitting an
other 5000 Heimwehr men into the
armed auxiliary service of the govern
ment yesterday Fey said there were
Stlli great reserves of man power to
draw on If they are needed.


report from Graz today said rail-
road men who betrayed the Syrian
Socialist leaders, Koloman and Wal
lisch, to police had been found slain
In nearby wood. Wallisch was
hanged February 10.


A rumor Of an attempt to assassi-
nate Chancellor Dollfuss was off,
cially denied.


The official organ of the Socialist
party today called upon followers to
be prepared to resume our fight"
The paper, the Arbeiter Zeitung, ap-
peared for the first time since the civil
war.


Streets Under Patrol.


Although Vienna continues quiet,
Heimwehr troopers again patrolled
the streets. with bayonets fixed, and
wearing steel helmets.


When martial law was lifted sew
eral days ago bayonets were ordered
sheathed and steel helmets were re-
placed by hats.


Preparations were being made to
try imprisoned Socialist leaders for
high treason. More than 1000 Social
lists are awaiting trial.


The semi-oficial Reichspost today
said 297 were killed in the civil war,
of which 81 were women and two
were children. This list was con-
siderably larger than the official one.


Unofficial estimates that the death
toll exceeded 1000 were called anti
Austrian propaganda" by the news
paper


The Arbeiter Zeitung, printed in
Brno, Czechslovakia, arrived through
the mails and was distributed to sub
scribers by Chancellor Engelbert Doll
fuss government mail carriers.


1t was announced, however. that
henceforth the paper would appear
weekly instead of daily.


"Dollfuss has conquered" the organ
editorialized, but opportunities for a
resumption of our fight for our
revenge and for our victory will come"

SUNBURY, Pa, April A. Three
Army flyers escaped injury last night
as they "bailed out" of an Army
bombing plane they, were "ferrying"
from Mitchell Field, Long Island, 10
Cleveland. Ohio, after one Of its two
motors failed.


The plane was not carrying mail


The occupants, Lieut.. Don H. Bax-
ter, Lieut.. M. H. Crumley and Pvt.

plane at an altitude of about 1000
feet and landed uninjured. The plane
crashed on hillside about two miles
west of Winfield. between Sunbury
and Lewisburg. and was destroyed by
fire.


Lieut.. Baxter is from Mitchell Field
and the others are stationed at Sell
fridge Field.


Baxter said the right motor had
been giving a little trouble and final
ly "conked out" He added the plane.
Keystone bi-motor bomber, type
B-6-A, had been in service for sew
eral years.


The aviators, unacquainted with the
territory, threw out flares near Sun
bury and again near Winfield. neforc

persons in the vicinity, who took them
to Sunbury.


The flyers, who left Mitchell Field
about o'clock yesterday afternoon,
went to a Sunbury hotel. where Bax-
ter said they would await further
orders.

Scores of workmen today were
clearing the city of windfalls and
broken limbs after the heaviest thun-
derstorm in more than year dealt
Washington's trees a severe blow yes
terday afternoon.


Other damage was comparatively
light, although one of at least four
lightning bolts dropped on the city
during the height of the storm par
alyzed the electrical system in the
huge new Post ONCE Building.
The building plunged into semi
darkness and elevator service was
suspended for Is minutes.
The bolt struck 13,000-volt trans
former on the top floor in the south
east section of the building. Almost
normal service was quickly resumed.
Wind Hits 5s Miles.
Curiously enough, the torrential
rain which accompanied a 58-mile
wind flooded only three or four eel
lars in the city. the Sewer Depart
ment reported. Heavy Summer storms
in previous years have given con-
siderable trouble on this score.


The outlook today was for additional
showers this afternoon and probably
tonight and tomorrow, with little
change in temperature. The mercury
| shortly before noon today stood at the
comfortable level of rs degrees.


The wind struck hardest near
Thirty-fourth street between Prospect
| avenue and N street, where six big
trees were uprooted and huge limbs
torn from several others. The force
of the gale, which blew 48 miles an
hour for minutes. was felt generally
throughout the city.


The Districts once Of Trees and
Parking received at least go calls after
trees or big limbs were blown INTO the
! streets or onto automobiles and
houses. No injuries were reported
from these accidents.


100 Clear Away Debris.


The District had almost 100 work.
men clearing away the debris yester-
day afternoon and this morning.
| equipped with motor cranes, trucks,
axes. saws and cables.


The wind uprooted six big shade
trees around the rejecting pool at the
Lincoln Memorial, at least four others
around Hams Point and two in Du-
pont Circle, the United States park
police reported. Two other large wind
falls were cleared away at Twenty
second and P streets.


The lightning drilled a hole IN a
smokestack of the wilkins Coffee Co.
on Rhode Island avenue between Fifth
and Sixth streets northeast and set
fire to a Government-owned dwelling
! in the first block of Portland street
northeast Firemen extinguished the
! blaze after it had done considerable
damage


| Lightning also ripped a chimney
and part of the roof from house in
the 400 block of Oneida place. Fire
men put out flames started by the
bolt and covered the damaged roof
with tarpaulin.


Several power wires were blown
down, including one at Hardwood road
and Michigan avenue northeast, and
another in the 370O block of Ingomar
| street.


The storm was general over this
section. At Baltimore almost an inch
and a half of rain fell. although the
precipitation here was only fraction
over an inch, accompanied by hail in
scattered sections.

MARSEILLE, France, October 10
Queen Marie went to her slain soldier
husband today, dry-eyed and firmly
erect.


She went "just as a Queen should" I"
of the navy. She spared herself
nothing"


When Queen Marie, a sister Of King
Carol of Rumania, learned at Brian
con the King had been assassinated,
she asked that he be left exactly as
he was and where he died. She found
him there, stretched out on a couch
in the police prefecture.


For 20 minutes she remained alone
with her dead, kneeling beside her
husbands body as Pietri and others
withdrew.


Tragic Strain Shows.


Marie was shaken by grief when
she learned of the death aboard her
train and tainted several times dur
ing the night. But when she arrived,
she apparently regained her COM
posure, although showing signs of the
tragic strain.


The Queen arrived in the early
dawn aboard a special train with only
four passengers. Nine. Edouard Her
riot, wife of the former premier,
caught the train along the line late
at night and tried to comfort her.
She brought with her black so the
Queen could arrive dressed in mourn
ing.


France Expresses Grief.


The only others were the lady-in-
waiting and Court Marshal Dimi-
triejevitch.


Pietri met the Queen and expressed
his and Frances grief. Then, walk
ing steadily between the court marshal
and Nine. J0uhannaud, wife OF the
Marsille prefect, who was with the
King when he died and who closed his
eyes, Marie entered an automobile and
was driven swiftly past bareheaded,
silent little groups to the prefecture
death chamber.


The Queen came from the room
haggard and shaken and apparently
near collapse. She controlled herself
and went to a room in Nine. Jouhan-
naud's apartment in the prefecture.

BALTIMORE. May l9.-Business in
Baltimore showed large increases in
practically all divisions during April
and early May over the same period
a year ago, despite slight decrease
under March figures. according to the
monthly report of the Association Of
Commerce.
