Harry Pouder. executive vice presi-
dent, declared:


Despite the undoubted progress
that has been made, business is still
very sensitive to outside influences,
and many programs are being held
in allegiance until the legislative sit
uation is cleared In Baltimore there
are steadily favorable trends in en-
ployment, pay rolls, general trade,
shipping, real estate and credit"
For post Office receipts, new CONNER
cial car sales. industrial power con-
sumption. industrial and commercial
gas consumption. export and vessel
movements the last month was the
best April since 1881, while in new
passenger car sales it was the best
individual month since July, 1881,
the report showed.

Internal revenue tax experts assigned
to the local banks were swamped
with business today, as bank customers
clamored for final advice in connec-
tion with their income tax returns.


Business has been excellent for
several days. but the climax came
today because the regulations call for
the filing of such returns tomorrow,
March IS That sent the 'last-minute
crowd" to the banks and Government
revenue offices for needed information.


Some of the banks had to get out
all their extra chairs to make patrons
comfortable as they awaited their
turns with the tax authorities. Some
customers had only one question, which
could be quickly answered, while
others were loaded with queries which
they fired off in rapid succession.


Patrons of the banks have appreciat-
ed the service more than ever this
year. New rules put out by the
Internal Revenue Bureau stress ac-
curacy. The Government can hold
persons liable who may give incorrect
information, this making bankers more
careful in their free advice on income
tax matters.


1t was said in the financial district
today that the tax men have never
been nearly as busy in past years as
they are now. For one reason or
another, said one fnancier, the public
seems especially anxious to have the
returns absolutely correct.

Holland for the preliminary hearing

dox and Detective Sergeant Walter

1t was not until they were passing

CHIMOPOVI, Second Mesa, Ariz.,
August 27.-Showers came to the
land of the Navajos today, but not
drop fell on the mesas of the Hopis
as Indian priests finished their third
snake dance.


The medicine men, anxiously scan
ming the clouds. wondered what was
wrong with their prayers.


They had danced for the rain gods
as their fathers had done every year
within the memory Of the most vener-
able Hopi They had been careful
that most of the snakes they carried
in their hands throughout the dances
were venomous rattlers, believed by
the Hopis to be the favorite mes
sengers Of the rain gods who live
under the hot sands of the desert.


Three times they had danced at
three cities of the mesalands.


They added their individual pray
ers today that the gods send rains to
revive withering crops and bring them
food for the long Winter.

SPRINGFIELD, Ill, April 21-The
Illinois Supreme Court today reversed
the conviction of Louis Alterie, Chi

knocked out all of the reputation
vagrancy" convictions obtained against
underworld leaders in Chicago last

1888 amendment to the vagrancy law,

criminal reputation"

for vagrancy proof of court records of
habitual convictions was necessary
rather than the mere testimony of po-
lice and others that the accused bore
a reputation as a criminal.


Alterie, the seventh gangster con-
victed under the vagrancy act, had
been at liberty on $4,000 bond pend
ing appeal, following his conviction
last october 18.

MINNEAPOLIS. September T.
Howard Guilford, former newspaper
editor and leader of a fight for free
dom Of the press, came into the spot
light again today-slain.


He was shot down by gunman last
night in fashion typical of the under
world his publications often attacked
I Guilford, 40 years old, was driving
his automobile along South Side
street, going home, when the killer
and his companion drove their car
alongside Guilford's, poked the muzzle
of a shotgun through an open window
and pulled the trigger


The charge struck the former editor
of the Saturday Press and the Pink
Sheet in the head. His death appar-
entity was instantaneous.


Gunmen Flee Quickly.


Then, after taking one quick look to
make sure the charge had killed their
victim. the gunmen sped away. There
was but one witness and he told police
the killers machine bore yellow license
plates.


Seven years ago Guilford was at
tackled by gunmen He was wounded
seriously, but recovered. Guilford's
publications often were devoted to at
tacks on gambling and other forms of
vice. He said he had been threatened.


The Saturday Press was involved in
the famous case of the Minnesota
,oauenope slInnresSion law which was
held unconstitutional by the United
States Supreme Court after twice being
upheld by the Minnesota Supreme
Court.


legislature Gave Power.

lature, gave a district judge, sitting as
a court of equity, power to suppress

scandalous and defamatory matter"

the Saturday Press was ordered

with former Gov. Theodore Christian
son, sought removal of Floyd B. Oh
son, then Hennepin County attorney
at Minneapolis. The petition charged

properly.
/ This effort was unsuccessful, but
Guilford continued his attacks on

eral months ago Guilford entered the

They, with at least go others,

port.

mand at waterfront territory.

BY the Associated Press.


ST. PAUL, April 4.-Floods that
took nine lives receded today, giving
residents Of Western Wisconsin and
Southeastern Minnesota their first op-
portunity to survey the heavy damage
to property.


Torrents Of rain that fell Monday
hit Wisconsin communities hardest.
Precipitation there ranged from 2 to
4 inches.


Three trainmen were crushed to
death at Hudson, Wis. when a freight
train was derailed; three persons were
drowned near Whitehall, Wis, when
a buggy carrying seven persons was
washed into a stream, and two men
and a woman were drowned near Eau
Claire and Spring Valley, Wis.


Twenty persons trapped all day in
a woolen mill at Chippewa Falls, Wis,
were rescued late last night when
Duncan Creek receded about three
feet. Ninety other employees fled the
building just in time yesterday morning.


Flood conditions still were serious
at Menomonie and Cedar Falls, where
the Red Cedar River was overfiowing
its banks behind dams. Attempts
were made last night to relieve the
situation at Menomonie by dynamit-
ing the dam there, but it withstood
several charges as the water slowly
rose.


Traffic was back to normal in some
sections today. while in others washed
out roads, bridges and railroad tracks
required the attention of repair crews.
There was heavy loss Of live stock
throughout the territory.

Nicholas Stefan, a farmer

partake.

cluSion, and summoned police.

he and his elleged mistress,
Eufosine Ghibu, had cooked
some of the flesh and served it
to the guests. The remainder Of
the body was found in the
kitchen.


Irate villagers attempted to
lynch the man and woman.
Stefan will die, Mile Ghibu will
recover.

text:
Editor McGill Commodity Service. Inc.


AUBURNDALE, Mass, May 5 Np)
Commodity prices, following slS
consecutive declines, registered an in
crease during the current week. Price
changes in every group were of a
limited character, but six groups sue
cessfully averaged higher, while five
declined and three remained un-
changed. Industrial activity is now
at seasonal peak and on the whole
production schedules for early May
are being generally maintained along
conservative lines, being held in close
alignment with demand inventories
of some raw materials are advancing
but through cooperative measures
the supply demand ratio is being
held within bounds.


Industrial prices failed to climb
upward and registered one of the
few declines that have been noted
since the first of the year. This
group still hangs 46 per cent above
the low point of last year.


Farm Prices Recover.


Agricultural prices, which since
early February have steadily declined
recovered during the last week as
price strength in wheat. corn, oats.
barley, rye, cotton, beans and fax
seed was noted. The only declines
were confined to eggs and wool.


Live stock prices climbed upward,
equaling the high that was reached
last March. The recovery was due
primarily to cattle. which advanced
over the 81 level, more than counter
acting the weakness noted in hogs
and lambs.


Building material advanced slightly
as lumber prices strengthened mod
erately.


Non-ferrous metals declined, the
reaction almost wholly being attrib-
utable to price weakness in tin.


Ferrous metals moved upward to a
new high during the week, due pri-
marily to an increase in the COM
posite price of pig iron. The advance
was only moderate, being modified
by weakness in steel scrap.


Fine textiles registered more weak
ness than any other group. Although
cotton was fractionally higher than
week ago, pronounced weakness fea-
tured silk. wool was cents lower.
while cotton yarns and some finished
goods moved downward.

EDMONTON. Alberta, July 7.-As
a result of one of the finest June
seasons in many years, Alberta is now
veritable garden through the wooded
sections in the central and northern
sections along the foothills from
south to north. Foliage growth is two
weeks in advance of recent years, and
frequent rains this month have kept
the countryside fresh and delightful


While the rains make side roads
somewhat difficult to travel, all main
highways of the province. including
1000 miles of graveled road, and link
ing up Summer and mountain resorts
with the main centers, are in good
condition for motor traffic, since these
are all-weather roads. Tourists plan
ming motor trips to Alberta resorts
need have no qualms concerning
weather conditions,


The Banff- -Windermere Highway.
one of the most noted scenic routes
on the continent, was opened officially
during the latter part of May, and is
already accommodating many tour
lists. The highway leads from Banff,
famous Alberta mountain resort,
southwestward into Yoho Park in
British Columbia and south toward
the United States border.

A pleasure trip down the Potomac
River in 50-foot yacht ended dis
astrously for a party of four early
yesterday morning when an explosion
seriously burned two women and de-
molished the craft


The yacht, the Greyhound, owned
by Hugh Smith, lawyer, with Offices
in the Southern Building, had aboard
a party consisting of Smith, Mr.. and
Mrs. Harold Martin of 2022 Sixteenth
street northwest. and Miss Ethel
Weakly of the Ambassador Apart
ments. AS it neared Shepherds Land
ing, opposite Alexandria, the men
were in the pilot house and the wom-
en- in the galley astern preparing food.


Suddenly there was terrific explo-
sion and the galley was enveloped in
flames. The men seized fire extin-
guishers and played the contents on
the fire, and the women ran through
the wall of flame, their clothing
ablaze. The men then threw the
women into the river and jumped
after them.


The explosion had been noticed
from the deck of the Coast Guard
cutter Fox, which lowered motor
whale boats. All four of the yachts
occupants were rescued and taken to
the landing of the Old Dominion
Boat Club. The women were removed
to the Alexandria General Hospital.


Meanwhile, the Greyhound, left to
navigate itself, ran aground near
Shepherds Landing and burned to the
waters edge. Her value was esti-
mated at about $4,000.


At the Alexandria Hospital today
it was said that both women would
recover.


Smith reported to police that when
he jumped into the river his wallet,
containing $187, washed away.


The cause of the explosion has not
been determined.

LITTLE AMERICA, Antarctica. jan
uary 30 Via Mackay RADIO The
collapse of a mountain of ice near the
flagship and the narrow escape of a
seaplane from a crash nearly spelled
disaster Yesterday for the second Ant
arctic expedition of Rear Admiral Rich
ard E. Byrd.


Yesterday morning the plane. which
will carry out most of the expeditions
exploratory work. had taken off for its
first flight when the men on ship, hor-
rified, noticed that both its skis were
hanging vertically from its undercar-
riage


But after anxious moments Pilot
June put her down in a bank of soft
snow. Two hours later the craft was
safely flown from the ship to the base
here


A few minutes before noon the
10,000-ton flagship. creeping along the
east side of the Bay of Whales seeking
a mooring place along the barrier, ap-
preached the landing place used in the
previous expedition.


Safety Doubted.


Admiral Byrd studied the roof of
the barrier. which rose sheer from the
waters edge. in places 70 feet high. and
asked the meterologist, What do you
think of the place? Does it seem safe
TO you?"


The next minute there was a sound
like a skyscraper collapsing and quar-
ter of mile of ice barrier tumbled
into the sea. about 200 yards away
from the ship.


The impact rocked the ship and a
hundred thousand tons of ice spread
fanwise over the water.


The ship subsequently swung back to
the edge of the bay ice, about two and
a half miles northwest of Little Amer
lea. 1t will unload there and survey
party was sent to mark a trail to the
base


The planes escape was just as dra-
matte.


Skis Dangling.
Friday morning Chief Pilot June,
Assistant Pilot Bolin and Radio Oper-
ator Hutcheson took off in the plane
for Little America Shortly after the
take-off it was noted that the huge
skis which replaced the pontoons were
dangling from their pedestals-cords
anchored in one end Of the wing struts
and at the other to the toes Of the
skis to keep them in place had not
been properly removed.


June, felt that something had hap
pened, and asked Hutcheson to radio
the flagship for information. Then be
came over the ship.


1t looked like a crash landing. when
Bolin saw that nothing could be done.
The ships doctor was sent ashore with
. first aid kit.


Then the plane swooped down. The
skis wobbled in the air. but pressure
was strong enough to keep them verti-
cal She safely ran out her momentum
in the soft snow


Since the hagship's arrival Thursday,
most of the hours have been sleepless,
because of the mishaps and efforts to
excavate the old camp and build new
roads to it from the ship.

A delightful program of Christmas

ming Music Club, Florence Howard,

nous "Alleluiah' chorus was well

dental solos were sung by Barbara

gracious act and thoroughly enjoyed
by the large company which filled the

Enthusiastically received. To Miss Davis
belongs much credit for good ac-
compartments in both the solo num-

Oxford and George Washington
University teams debated the business
Of armament manufacture last night,
one seeking to prove the business
should be nationalized and the other
that it should not.


Speaking before an audience Of ap-
proximately 500 persons in Stockton
Hall, the debaters joined in condemn
ing private manufacture for profit,
but disagreed on the proper solution of
the problem.


Oxford upheld the affirmative and
George Washington the negative of
the question: Resolved that this
house favors the naturalization of
armament production"


Temptation Too Great"


The oxford speakers, Michael Foot
and John Stafford Cripps. argued that
"the existence of q system Of private
manufacture of arms confers upon in
dividuals powers too great for indi-
viduals to control, and temptations
too great for individuals to resist"


Without naturalization, they said,
work for world peace never can sue
coed and present efforts are rendered
hypocritical and false. The removal
Of private individuals from arms manu-
facture would make 1t possible to fix
responsibility and to focus public opin-
ion more effectually upon the preven-
ton Of war, they maintained.


Licensing Urged.


Arguing against naturalization Of
the industry, the George Washington
speakers, Dix Price and Arthur Muir
ply, painted an even blacker picture
than did the Britishers of bribery and
other nefarious practices in the manu-
facture and sale Of arms.


Drawing literally from the revela-
tionS of the recent Senate investiga-
tions, they said that governments have
taken an equal part with manufac-
turers in selling war" and contended
that to turn the industry over to
government would only remove one
Of the partners without correcting the
abuses. They advocated, instead, a
system Of licensing.


The audience was left to draw its
own conclusions from the debate, no
decision being rendered. Prof. Charles
s. Collier of the George Washington
law faculty presided.

CHICAGO, August 1S-The sensa-
tional rise of hog prices at the Ma
tion's leading live stock markets dur
ing the last three weeks today had
lifted swine values to the highest
prices in three years.


With more than $3.50, including
the Government processing tax, be-
ing paid at some Eastern markets,
the price levels show an advance of
as much as $125 during this week
and are more than So above the late
May low figure.


Market quotations here are the
highest since September, 1881, and
with the tax of $225 per hundred
weight, the current cost to packers has
not been equaled since November, 1880.


81 Millions Already Paid.


The tax goes into the Government
fund used to pay benefits to farmers
who cooperate in the corn-hog pro-
gram. More than $31,000,000 has
been paid out already under this law.


Today's market here was little more
than the usual Saturday affair. Only
500 animals we're received for the
commercial trade, and these went at
prices steady with yesterday, about 5
cents below the top of $6.65. The
average price of hogs now is $500
against $485 last week and $685. last
year. These prices do not include
the tax.


Sharp curtailment of hog receipts,
caused, according to some trade in
terests, by the drought and the swine
reduction program of last Fall, was
the principal factor in the rush to
acquire hogs. Added to this was the
fact that pork prices have increased
steadily to a level now about so per
cent higher than year ago.


Supplies at Low Ebb.


The huge reduction in receipts
this week amounted to approximately
LOO 900 head as compared with the
corresponding week a year ago at
leading markets. Compared with last
week, principal markets had about
10000 fewer hogs. Slaughter supplies
over the entire country are averaging
the smallest of the year. Available
fresh receipts in many places are not
sufficient to take care of the current
demand.

R.-Commodity prices during the past
week again averaged higher, represent

upSwing has lost momentum during the

much less pronounced, is well illustrated

decline in hides and leather, non-fer-

cal with the previous week. During

Anna Antonio, who hated her
husband but loved her children,
was finished today. Anna Is
dead.


Three times they reprieved her.


And then last night they har-
messed her frail, self.starved body

him. When he left, his mother
gave him the rubber ball and an
apple.


She would not let the older
children see her for fear they
might guess at her fate.


When her time was called, Mrs.
Antonio walked bravely from her
cell along with Father Francis
McCaffrey, the prison chaplain.
She carried crucifix.


In Snyder Cell

cupied by Ruth Snyder, also ex-
ecuted for killing her husband for

District license act.


There are about 5000 structures

hotels. theaters and places of public
assembly. Because considerable time
is required for making annual in
spections. the policy was adopted
of allowing owners to make license
payments in advance of inspections.

changes in structures deemed neces-
sary. In the past year. Dram said,
more than 100 refused to comply.

fees would not be accepted until cor
rections were made About q dozen
since have complied.


The others, Capt. Dram said, will
be taken to court and may be fined.

until regulations were accepted.


He said it has been impossible to
make all inspections before the be-
ginning of the license year because
of the small force of inspectors and

The back-to- tle-land movement and the
movement to link part-time industrial activity
with part-time work on the farm, one OF the
proposed solutions of the unemployment prob
lem already is under way on really appre-
ciable scale.


An analysis of figures obtained by the Gen.
sus Bureau in Is Eastern, Southern and Gen.
tral States disclosed many lines of activities In
which persons living on farms obtained outside
income to aid in meeting their living expenses
and supplying cash for those demands for
which farmer must have ready money.


In the census from which the figures were
obtained it was found that in the Is States
studied. 900 people were employed at
part-time factory work. Many also did work
for factories at home sold raw materials
required by the small industries for their prod
ucts.


The factories included textile mills paper
plants canning factories. meat-packing plants,
machine shops. leather factories, clay and glass
industries. Some Of the factories are owned
entirely by farm people, some are financed in
part by farm people More than half the fac
tories surveyed are in North Carolina, Pennsyl-
vania and Virginia; there is good representa-
ton in West Virginia, Massachusetts, and New
York. and the remainder are scattered gener-
ally throughout the area covered by the survey.


The bureau reports that most of the farmers





receiving some income their investments,
and that the existence of the factories afforded
an expanded outlet for locally produced fruits,
vegetables eggs, poultry. milk and other farm
products. Most of the farm people working
for wages in the factories were receiving from
$500 to 81 900 in wages per worker. there were
many part-time workers who received $50 to
$500 year. and a few farm people were fac
tory superintendents who received around
$4,000 a year.


The bureau reports that outside employment
of farm people is especially pronounced in areas
where small farms are numerous and where
agriculture is handicapped by unfavorable nat
ural resources. Its survey excluded the subsist-
junct of industrial employment, and included
only people living on farms as defined by the
census.


Some of the farm people interviewed in the
bureaus current survey said that were it not
for the income received from outside industrial
work they would have to quit farming, others
that the local industrial employment kept young
people on the farm. Some complaint was voiced
that wages were too low, but the consensus was
that the farm people, employed even in part
time industrial work were better off, financially
and socially. than if they lived in the city.

Marinus Van der Lubbe. 24-year-old
Dutch stonemason. was beheaded to-

He had repeatedly confessed setting

Van der Lubbe had been under SEN

Steps through which the Dutch gov

Late last night Van der Lubbe was
informed by the Leipzig prison governor

from the stupor in which he remained
virtually throughout the long trial.


Van der Lubbe did not reply to the

MICHIGAN CITY, Ind, April 23.-
Four prisoners, three of them serving
life terms. escaped from the Michigan
City prison during the week end,
prison officials revealed today.


Leland Phillips, 26, serving life
term for murder, and Noah Seals,
serving three-year sentence for sec
ond-degree burglary escaped some
time Saturday from the prison farm
west of Michigan City. Both are
white men.


Cook and Janitor Escape.


Two colored men, Willard Butler,
81, and Charles Irwin, 38, both serv-
ing life terms for murder, escaped
Sunday. Butler had been employed
as cook at the home of Warden Louis
Kunkel on the prison grounds and
Irwin was a janitor in the prison bar
ber shop.


Butler and Irwin had only to walk
away from the prison, as their duties
took them beyond the institution
walls.


Phillips and Seals, however, were
reported to have been under guard at
the farm, to which they had been de-
tailed for special work.


Probe to Be Made.


Warden Kunkel said an investiga-
ton would be made to determine how
Phillips and Seals escaped.


Phillips was sentenced to the prison
in September, 1926, from Richmond
for the Staying of Frank Buck. But
Ter was sentenced from Danville
Hendricks County, in September,
1925; Irwin from Indianapolis in
September. 1922. and Seals from
Rockport, Spencer County, in Sep
tember, 1892


Police of the various cities were
notified Of the escape of the prisoners
and were asked to watch for them.

The automobile industry moved
swiftly today toward a general
wage increase and shorter work.
ing hours for it's half million
workers.

return, yesterday, to his pre-de-
preston minimum wage of SIS a
day, the National Automobile

mended that it's member COM
panies adopt the 36-hour week,
hire 10000 additional men, and
raise wages to compensate for the
shorter hours.


Make Union Issue


At the same time the chamber
issued a statement serving notice
on the Federal Government and
the labor unions that the manu-
facturerS intend to make an issue
of the dispute over company
unions.


The statement said members of
the trade group would continue to
meet and bargain collectively with
employees representatives whether
those representatives represent
the majority of employees minor
ity groups or individuals.


Answers Roosevelt Appeal

would affect about 95 per cent Of
all workers employed by the auto
bile companies. The small per-
centage excluded from the wage
and hour revision are office work
erS, clerks, accountants and va
rious high-salaried experts.


The chamber statement Specifi-
cally said the new policy was be-
ing recommended to the compa-
nies in response to the appeal Of
President Roosevelt.

AUBURNDALE, Mass, July 21-
Commodity prices during the third
week in July again moved upward.
Agricultural prices, which have shown
a marked disposition to increase this
month as a result of extended drought
and crop deterioration, were the chief
causation behind the higher price
average. Data now available clearly
shows that final production of both
feed and bread grains will rule the
lowest on modern records. During the
week, the trend of individual groups
was mixed. Out of IA individual
groups. five advanced, declined, and
7 remained unchanged.


Industrial commodities showed an
advance, breaking the horizontal trend
which has BEEN in effect for the past
few months and bringing the index TO
the highest point recorded so far this
year. A further contraction in in
dustrial activity during the third
week of the month was Of a fairly
limited character, and reflects sea-
sonal characteristics.


Farm Prices Advance.


Agricultural prices showed the
greatest proportionate advance Of any
group. Again the price recovery was
primarily due to grains and cotton.
The material strengthening in the
statistical position has resulted in
considerable speculative activity. Dur
ing the week, the items that ruled
higher were as follows: Wheat corn,
oats, rye, cotton, eggs. hay and flax
seed, with no commodities recording
declines.


Live stock prices brought the index
slightly above that Of last week, with
cattle and lambs down, but more than
offset by an increase in hogs and
sheep.


Paint materials declined during the
week due to lower prices for linseed

prices for cotton, cotton goods and
yarns o..

itic rioting by the Arab popula-
ton, which in Constantine and
nearby cities has cost scores Of
lives amid scenes Of indescribable
horror.


Deny Riots Spreading


The officials meanwhile denied
the rioting had spread widely to
other Algerian cities and towns.


There had been rioting at Ain
Beida, so miles from Constantine,
on Monday, they admitted, in
which Jewish houses were burned
and 13 wounded, including five
Jewish men, six Jewish women,
one Arab and one native child.
They denied that there had been
deaths at Ain+Beida, as elsewhere
reported.


There was no inclination to
minimize the seriousness of the
situation, however, as sickening
reports Of the mutilations suf-
tered by the Jews came in.


Among the Jewish dead in the
morgue at Constantine were four
children under 10 years of age.
One was a 2-year-old baby. All
had their throatS cut.


Troops Patrol AIgiers
With much larger Jewish
population here, any outbreak in
Alg1ers would be even more serious
than the one in Constantine. How
ever, with the French authorities
realizing the situation and troops
with rifles parading the Ghetto,
one did not seem likely.


The intelligence department of
the French administration is in
vestigating to discover what new
influence among the Arabs turned
the common street fighting be-
tween the Arabs and the Jews
into such a horrible manifestation
Of bloodthirsty race warfare.

been seen in Catalonia recently. At
tempts to learn his whereabouts
through French officials proved fruit
less.

A list Of approximately a
thousand junior high school stu

under the emergency relief regu-
lationS is being checked today by
Miss Alice Hill, director of
emergency relief, following a a'esn'
plant that these pupils had
been overlooked in the distriblS
ton of school lunches.


Relief officials said today that
the original plans for school
lunches received by them from
school officials did not contain
any mention of junior high
school boys and girls and that
plans had been made for noon
day meals to relief children in
graded schools only.


When the oversight was re.
ported several days ago an effort
was made to get additional FERA
funds for this purpose for October,
but Federal officials refused to
supplement the original $4,000
earmarked for school meals this
month.


The plan at present is to provide
junior high school lunches and

being out of school cafeteria
profits. District relief officials
will ask for adequate funds tor all
school lunches for next month and
ensuing periods.

FALSE PASS. Alaska, August B.
Seven malemute pups, whelped two
months ago in a volcano while Father
Bernard Hubbard. the glacier priest.
and his party were trekking into the
unexplored Aghileen Pinnacles region,
are back at the base camp with
a story as exciting as that Of the
seven men they accompanied.


The pups travelled for a month
by dog back. being carried in pack
sacks by Margie, their mother, pride
Of Father Hubbard's dog team, and
by Matmai, another of the malemutes
accompanying in the party in the Paw
Low volcano region Of the Alaska Pen
insula.


Their canine taxis took them
through swamps, over mountain ridges
and through rivers swollen to flood
stage.


On the outward trek, Margie, carry
ing four Of her pups in a pack sack,
strayed from the party and discovery
of her absence was not made until
more than five hours after she disap-
peared.


Fearing loss of the mother and
pups by exposure or a brown bear
attack, the party made temporary camp
for the night and the next morning
rescue and search party. composed
of Edgar Levin, Kenneth Chisholm,
and Wolf. another malemute, back
tracked for eight hours to locate the
missing dogs.


VOLTS keen nose located one stray
pup and later the remaining trio and
their mother were found near the
spot where they last had been seen.


They were none the worse after a
cold night spent in the swamps.
